description.p: A question that cannot be answered in the terms it was asked.

section.label: Source
section.p: Mumonkan (Wumenguan, The Gateless Gate), case 1, compiled by Wumen Huikai and published in 1228. The exchange belongs to the Tang master Zhaozhou Congshen (Jp. Jōshū), and is recorded in earlier collections. Wumen's commentary and verse are his own.

section.label: Scene
section.p: A monk asks Zhaozhou whether a dog has Buddha-nature. Zhaozhou answers "Mu", meaning no, or nothing. Orthodox doctrine holds that all beings have Buddha-nature, so the answer contradicts the teaching the monk expected. Wumen's commentary tells the student to pass the barrier with the whole body and mind, to avoid reading Mu as nothingness or as a yes-or-no, and to carry it like a hot iron ball that cannot be swallowed or spat out.

section.label: Symbols
section.p: The gate is the barrier of the patriarchs, and it has no gate in the sense of a door: the only way through is the question itself. The dog is an ordinary creature that the monk's doctrine has already classified. The syllable Mu is a negation with nothing behind it, and it is used as the object of sustained attention in Rinzai practice. The card is unnumbered because it belongs to no sequence.

section.label: Teaching
section.p: Mu is the head phrase (wato, 話頭) on which attention is gathered until the "great doubt" (daigi, 大疑) forms. The tradition treats the first koan as the entrance to the whole curriculum. The case turns on shūjō (衆生) and busshō (佛性), sentient beings and Buddha-nature, and on the habit of settling such questions by concept.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A question that cannot be answered in the terms it was asked. The card marks a beginning before any plan exists and invites sustained attention to the question instead of a quick resolution. It can also name a refusal to be classified.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Treating Mu as a technique for producing a state, or as a clever denial. Wumen warns against both the nihilist reading (a void) and the reading that sets being against non-being. The opposite error is to collect the answer as a piece of knowledge.

section.label: Links
section.p: I — Searching for the Ox: the seeker who has not yet heard the question as his own. VIII — The Ox and the Man Both Gone Out of Sight: Mu is where the emptiness of that card is first met. XV — Ordinary Mind: Zhaozhou carries the same plain manner into his own answer to Nanquan.

description.p: A sense of lack with no object, or a search whose object cannot yet be named.

section.label: Source
section.p: Kuoan Shiyuan (Jp. Kakuan), Ten Ox-Herding Pictures, picture 1; 12th century, Song China. The paintings most often reproduced are attributed to Tenshō Shūbun (1414–1463). Kuoan wrote the prose preface and verse for each picture.

section.label: Scene
section.p: A herdsman goes alone into wilderness, through grass, rivers and mountain paths, looking for an ox he has lost. Kuoan's preface says the ox was never lost: the man has estranged himself from his own nature, and desire and fear unsettle him. In the verse he is exhausted, with a long road ahead, and hears only cicadas in the maples. The picture shows no ox.

section.label: Symbols
section.p: The ox stands for true nature or mind, the herdsman for the practitioner. The wilderness is the world of pursuit, and the missing ox is the thing sought. Its absence from the picture is the point: nothing in the scene yet shows what is being looked for. The cicadas mark late summer and a noise that goes on regardless.

section.label: Teaching
section.p: The doctrine is that Buddha-nature (busshō) is present from the start, so the search starts from a false premise that is nevertheless the only way in. The Chinese title of the stage, xún niú, means seeking the ox. The restlessness is a form of kleśa, affliction, which Kuoan names as desire and fear.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A sense of lack with no object, or a search whose object cannot yet be named. The card does not predict success. It names the disposition from which a path begins, and it asks what is being sought and whether it is elsewhere.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Equating the search with the result: more seeking, more teachers, more books, with each new method a way of staying lost. Another is to take the preface's reassurance as a reason not to seek at all.

section.label: Links
section.p: 0 — Mu: the question that sends the seeker out. II — Seeing the Traces: the next stage, in which texts give the first signs. X — Entering the Market with Open Hands: the cycle returns here, and the figure who returns can search without the old distress.

description.p: Early evidence that something is there: a book, a teacher, a remark that rings true.

section.label: Source
section.p: Kuoan Shiyuan, Ten Ox-Herding Pictures, picture 2; 12th century.

section.label: Scene
section.p: The herdsman finds hoofprints beside a stream and under the trees. In the preface, scripture and teaching have shown him the traces: he sees that all things share one substance and that the world reflects the self, but he cannot yet tell right from wrong. The verse says the animal may have wandered far, yet its scent rises to the sky and cannot be hidden.

section.label: Symbols
section.p: The footprints are the teachings, sutras and the words of teachers, which point to the ox without being the ox. The stream and trees are the same landscape as in the first picture, now carrying evidence. The herdsman bends toward the ground and looks at marks, which is the posture of study.

section.label: Teaching
section.p: The stage corresponds to learning and doctrine, kyōgaku (教學) in Japanese usage, and to the first understanding of non-duality at the level of concept. Zen holds that this understanding is real but insufficient. The preface's admission that the seeker cannot yet tell right from wrong marks the gap between knowing a doctrine and acting from it.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Early evidence that something is there: a book, a teacher, a remark that rings true. The card suggests following the evidence while remembering that signs are not the thing they indicate. It can name a period of study.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Mistaking the traces for the ox: collecting doctrine and becoming learned without a first-hand experience. Zen's slogan of a transmission "not founded on words and letters" targets this stage.

section.label: Links
section.p: I — Searching for the Ox: the same seeker, now with something to follow. III — Seeing the Ox: the traces lead to a direct sight. XI — The Flower and the Smile: the tradition's own account of a teaching that goes beyond scripture.

description.p: A sudden clarity that is real and carries no guarantee that it will last.

section.label: Source
section.p: Kuoan Shiyuan, Ten Ox-Herding Pictures, picture 3; 12th century.

section.label: Scene
section.p: The herdsman sees the ox, standing alone in a spring landscape. A nightingale sings on a branch, the willows are green and the sun is warm, and the ox has nowhere to hide. The preface says he now hears the way, the senses are in harmony, and the ox's presence pervades everything like salt dissolved in water. When he looks rightly, he finds it is himself.

section.label: Symbols
section.p: The ox appears for the first time, often partly hidden, as in a first glimpse. The birdsong shows the sense of hearing opened, and the willows and sun show a world made vivid. Salt in water is the preface's image for something present everywhere and visible nowhere as a separate object.

section.label: Teaching
section.p: This is the first kenshō (見性), literally seeing into one's nature, in the Japanese tradition's terms. The preface places the entry through the senses and states the identity of seer and seen. Rinzai teaching treats kenshō as a beginning that needs long cultivation.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A sudden clarity: a moment when something becomes obvious. The card says the glimpse is real and gives no guarantee that it will last. It invites the reader to keep what was seen without building a story around it.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Taking the first glimpse for the whole of the path, announcing it, or ranking oneself by it. Zen teachers speak of "stinking of Zen" (zen kusai, 禅臭い), the air that clings to those who display their attainment.

section.label: Links
section.p: II — Seeing the Traces: the study that preceded the sight. IV — Catching the Ox: the glimpse has to be taken hold of. VII — The Ox Forgotten: the ox seen here is the one that later disappears.

description.p: A struggle to hold on to something seen, against habits that return quickly.

section.label: Source
section.p: Kuoan Shiyuan, Ten Ox-Herding Pictures, picture 4; 12th century.

section.label: Scene
section.p: The herdsman has the ox, but it is wild and resists, longing for its old pasture. In the verse he has seized it with all his strength and its will is fierce; it struts up the plateau, then vanishes into a misty pass. The preface says full mastery needs a firm use of the whip.

section.label: Symbols
section.p: The rope appears in hand for the first time, and the preface calls for the whip. The rope is attention, the whip is effort and discipline, and the ox's resistance is the habit-energy of the old mind. The mist in the pass shows how quickly the experience of the third picture can slip away.

section.label: Teaching
section.p: The stage describes the work of stabilising an insight against habitual patterns: karma and the traces of past conditioning (Skt. vāsanā). In Rinzai practice it corresponds to the long koan work after the first kenshō. The preface treats effort here as necessary, not as a sign of error.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A period of struggle to hold on to something seen: a decision, a resolution, a new way of working. The card asks for steady effort and some force, and it warns that the old habits return quickly.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Holding too hard. The force that catches the ox can harden into a fixation that prevents its calming. The opposite error is giving up when the insight proves unstable.

section.label: Links
section.p: III — Seeing the Ox: the sight that must now be held. V — Herding the Ox: the struggle softens into routine. XVI — The Wild Fox: the consequences of mistaken freedom from cause and effect.

description.p: Disciplined, steady, unglamorous work; progress through regularity.

section.label: Source
section.p: Kuoan Shiyuan, Ten Ox-Herding Pictures, picture 5; 12th century.

section.label: Scene
section.p: The herdsman leads the ox with a nose-string and whip, and the ox walks beside him. The preface says that one thought arises after another in an unending chain; clarity makes them true and confusion makes them false. The verse warns that if he slackens whip and tether, the ox will wander into the dust. Tended properly, it becomes docile and follows without a chain.

section.label: Symbols
section.p: The nose-string is mindfulness, and the whip is the correction that follows a lapse. The ox walks on, still tethered, and the grass is the ordinary world of sense objects. The change from the fourth picture is that the ox now cooperates.

section.label: Teaching
section.p: The picture shows shugyō (修行), practice after awakening, and the Zen teaching that realisation must be matured. The preface's remark about the chain of thought refers to the arising of mental activity (nen, 念) and to the work of discernment. Dōgen's idea that practice and realisation are one is relevant to the later stages.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Disciplined, steady, unglamorous work. The card names a stretch in which progress comes from regularity, and it favours routine over breakthrough.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Taking discipline as the goal: formal rigidity, the "stinking" posture of one who guards his purity. The preface's own condition for release is that the tether eventually becomes unnecessary.

section.label: Links
section.p: IV — Catching the Ox: the same animal, now broken to the lead. VI — Riding the Ox Home: the tether is loosened. XV — Ordinary Mind: the later form of discipline that no longer looks like discipline.

description.p: Ease after effort, with practice and life in agreement.

section.label: Source
section.p: Kuoan Shiyuan, Ten Ox-Herding Pictures, picture 6; 12th century. The Chinese title is literally "riding the ox, returning home."

section.label: Scene
section.p: The struggle is over and the herdsman sits on the ox's back, playing a flute on the way home through the evening mist. The preface says gain and loss no longer concern him, and he hums rustic tunes and ignores calls to turn back. The verse describes a joy that cannot be put into words.

section.label: Symbols
section.p: The flute and the ride are ease, and the ox is now a mount instead of an opponent. The evening mist is the dusk of effort, and home is the original nature. The herdsman's eyes are fixed ahead. In some paintings the whip lies unused.

section.label: Teaching
section.p: The stage describes harmony between practitioner and mind, with the dualism of striver and struggled-against beginning to dissolve. The preface's indifference to gain and loss corresponds to the Buddhist ideal of equanimity (upekṣā).

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Ease after effort, with practice and life in agreement. The card suggests the work has been absorbed and invites the reader to enjoy it without watching it.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Contentment, the attachment to a pleasant state of mind. The herdsman is still riding, and the ox is still there: the dualism remains, and the music can become the new object of desire.

section.label: Links
section.p: V — Herding the Ox: the discipline that made this ease possible. VII — The Ox Forgotten: the animal is dropped once home is reached. X — Entering the Market with Open Hands: the same lightness, extended to others.

card.title: The Ox Forgotten, Leaving the Man Alone

description.p: The tool has done its work and can be put down.

section.label: Source
section.p: Kuoan Shiyuan, Ten Ox-Herding Pictures, picture 7; 12th century.

section.label: Scene
section.p: The herdsman has reached home and the ox is gone. He sits at ease in the thatched hut, and the whip and rope lie idle. The preface says the ox was a symbol: once the hare is caught, the snare is forgotten, and gold is separated from dross like the moon coming out of clouds. In the verse, he sleeps late into the day.

section.label: Symbols
section.p: The empty field and the idle tools show that the means is no longer needed. The snare and the hare come from the Zhuangzi, which Kuoan's preface echoes. The rising moon stands for clarity coming out of obscuring cloud. The herdsman remains, which is the stage's limit.

section.label: Teaching
section.p: The doctrine is upāya (方便, hōben), skilful means, and the principle that teachings are a raft to be left on the shore. The means is dropped but the self who used it persists, so the stage still contains a subject. The problem of the self remains.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: The tool has done its work and can be put down: a method, a role, a belief. The card suggests that a long effort has ended in a plain satisfaction and invites asking what remains once the scaffolding goes.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Pride in having let go. A person who has dropped the ox may rest on that and refuse the next step, where the person also drops.

section.label: Links
section.p: VI — Riding the Ox Home: the animal that has just been left behind. VIII — The Ox and the Man Both Gone Out of Sight: the self follows the ox. XIII — Pacifying the Mind: the mind sought and not found.

card.title: The Ox and the Man Both Gone Out of Sight

description.p: A clearing in which roles, goals and the self that held them lose their grip.

section.label: Source
section.p: Kuoan Shiyuan, Ten Ox-Herding Pictures, picture 8; 12th century. The picture is an empty circle (ensō, 圓相). The earlier Puming series ends at an empty circle, whereas Kuoan continues past it.

section.label: Scene
section.p: Whip, rope, ox and man have all disappeared. The preface says confusion has cleared and only serenity remains, without even the idea of holiness; where there is no duality, not even a thousand eyes could find a gap, and a holiness that birds would honour with flowers is an embarrassment. In the verse, no one can survey the vastness of heaven, and a snowflake cannot fall on a blazing furnace.

section.label: Symbols
section.p: In Kuoan's picture the circle is a blank; this deck shows it as an empty clearing, with the ground and a few trees and no one in it. It stands for emptiness (śūnyatā, kū, 空), wholeness and the completion of a movement, and in Zen painting the brush circle is a signature of the artist's state at the moment of drawing. The furnace and snowflake show a mind in which nothing lodges.

section.label: Teaching
section.p: The doctrine is the dropping of subject and object together (jingyū gubō), the emptiness of both self and means. The Heart Sutra's "form is emptiness" belongs to this stage. Dongshan's Five Ranks give a parallel in the first rank, the relative within the absolute, where particulars are absorbed into emptiness.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A clearing: a phase in which roles, goals and the self that held them lose their grip. The card can mean a real relief, a pause before a new form, or a state with no content that is not yet a state of understanding.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Attachment to emptiness. Hakuin, among other teachers, warned against the "cave of the black mountain" (kokuzan kikutsu, 黒山鬼窟), the dead quiet in which a practitioner sits as if awakened, with nothing in his life changed. The picture is the limit of the Puming series, and Kuoan's continuation exists to prevent a stop here.

section.label: Links
section.p: VII — The Ox Forgotten: the step before, where the self still remains. IX — Returning to the Source: the world reappears. 0 — Mu: the blank that opened the whole sequence.

description.p: Seeing the situation as it is, without commentary.

section.label: Source
section.p: Kuoan Shiyuan, Ten Ox-Herding Pictures, picture 9; 12th century.

section.label: Scene
section.p: The herdsman sits in his hut, or is absent, while water flows and flowers bloom. In the preface he has been pure from the beginning and untouched by defilement; he watches things grow and change from a stillness that does not move, and he does not identify with their illusory transformations. The verse says that returning to the origin is itself a false step, and that it would be better to stay at home; the streams flow of their own accord, and the flowers are red, for no one in particular.

section.label: Symbols
section.p: The river and the flowers represent the phenomenal world, seen with nothing added. Green mountains and blue water appear in the preface as things as they are. Some versions of the picture show only landscape, with no person.

section.label: Teaching
section.p: The stage corresponds to the saying, attributed to Qingyuan Weixin, that before practice mountains are mountains, during practice they are not, and after realisation they are again. The Chinese terms for source and origin (ben, yuan) refer to the original ground, and the doctrine in play is the second half of the Heart Sutra's formula, "emptiness is form" (kū soku ze shiki, 空即是色), together with the Mahāyāna principle that saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are not two.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Seeing the situation as it is, without commentary: clear perception after a period of confusion. The card suggests that nothing needs adding and invites the reader to look at what is already present.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Quietism: remaining in the hut and letting the world run on without taking part. The verse's own irony, that "returning" is already a step too many, warns against making a project of this stage as well.

section.label: Links
section.p: VIII — The Ox and the Man Both Gone: the emptiness out of which the world re-emerges. X — Entering the Market with Open Hands: the clear seer goes out. XV — Ordinary Mind: the same recovery of the plain world, in a master's words.

card.title: Entering the Market with Open Hands

description.p: Returning to ordinary life and being useful there without announcing it.

section.label: Source
section.p: Kuoan Shiyuan, Ten Ox-Herding Pictures, picture 10; 12th century. The figure is conventionally read as Budai (Jp. Hotei), the laughing monk of 10th-century China, though Kuoan's text does not name him.

section.label: Scene
section.p: The herdsman, barefoot and bare-chested, goes into the marketplace carrying a gourd and leaning on a staff. The preface says his gate is closed and even the wise cannot see into him; he mingles with drunkards and butchers, and they become Buddhas. In the verse his face and chest are smeared with mud and ashes, he smiles broadly, and he makes dead trees bloom without using supernatural powers.

section.label: Symbols
section.p: The market is the ordinary world of trade and appetite. The gourd and staff are the travelling monk's equipment, and the bare feet show that he has no rank. The open hands (suishu, 垂手, literally hands hanging down) give without grasping. Budai's sack and belly come from his legend.

section.label: Teaching
section.p: The stage corresponds to the bodhisattva vow to work for the awakening of all beings, and to upāya. The idea is that realisation shows in conduct among others, with no outward sign of distinction. The tradition calls the work after awakening gogo no shugyō (悟後の修行).

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Returning to ordinary life with whatever has been learned, and being useful there without announcing it. The card may point to teaching, caring for others, or joining a community. It also marks the close of a cycle, and the next card is the first.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: A show of humility, or a missionary stance that sets the helper above the helped. The preface says the figure's goodness is invisible, which excludes the performance of it.

section.label: Links
section.p: I — Searching for the Ox: the cycle returns, and the seeker begins again. IX — Returning to the Source: the clear sight that makes this possible. XVII — The Shout: another form of acting for others, much less gentle.

description.p: A recognition that passes between two people without explanation.

section.label: Source
section.p: Mumonkan case 6, Wumen Huikai, 1228. The Flower Sermon is a legend. It is first attested in 1036, in a Chinese Chan text, and no Indian source contains it. Scholars treat it as a later Chan invention that grounds the claim of a transmission outside the scriptures in the Buddha himself.

section.label: Scene
section.p: On Vulture Peak, the Buddha holds up a flower to his assembly and says nothing. The monks are puzzled, and only Mahākāśyapa smiles. The Buddha then says that he holds the true dharma eye, the wondrous mind of nirvana, and entrusts it to Mahākāśyapa. Wumen's commentary jokes that Gautama passed dog's meat off as mutton, and asks what would have happened to the transmission if everyone had smiled, or no one.

section.label: Symbols
section.p: The flower is the teaching in its simplest form, with no argument or text. The smile is recognition without words. The assembly's silence is the audience that failed to see. Mahākāśyapa, the disciple foremost in ascetic practice, is counted as the first patriarch of the lineage.

section.label: Teaching
section.p: The case grounds the Chan formula of "a special transmission outside the scriptures" (教外別傳, kyōge betsuden) and the idea of mind-to-mind transmission (ishin denshin, 以心傳心). The doctrinal point is that the dharma is not stored in the words of the sutras.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A recognition that passes between two people without explanation, or the beginning of a line of inheritance. The card can also name the experience of being the only one in a room to understand, and what follows from it.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: The cult of the wordless: treating silence as superior to speech, or using claims of inexpressible understanding to avoid examination. Wumen's joke addresses this, and the later Chan literature is full of words.

section.label: Links
section.p: II — Seeing the Traces: scripture as traces, set against transmission outside it. XII — Facing the Wall: the legend of the next patriarch in the line. XV — Ordinary Mind: the later form of mind-to-mind transmission, in everyday speech.

description.p: A refusal to explain; solitude in the service of a long task.

section.label: Source
section.p: Blue Cliff Record case 1, with verse by Xuedou Chongxian and commentary by Yuanwu Keqin, dated 1125. The nine years of wall-gazing at Shaolin are reported in later Chan histories such as the Anthology of the Patriarchal Hall (952). Bodhidharma is a semi-legendary figure, and much of his biography was added after the 6th century. The four-line verse "a special transmission outside the scriptures, not founded on words and letters, pointing directly at the mind, seeing one's nature and becoming a Buddha" is attributed to him but first appears as a single verse in the Zuting shiyuan of 1108; the attribution is later.

section.label: Scene
section.p: Emperor Wu of Liang, a patron of Buddhism, asks Bodhidharma what the highest meaning of the holy truths is. The answer is that there is vast emptiness and nothing holy. Asked who it is that stands before him, Bodhidharma says he does not know. The emperor fails to understand, and Bodhidharma crosses the Yangtze and goes north to the kingdom of Wei. Zhigong tells the emperor that the man was Avalokiteśvara, and that no one could bring him back. In the legend, Bodhidharma then sits facing a wall at Shaolin for nine years.

section.label: Symbols
section.p: The wall is the opaque surface on which attention rests, the barrier and the support. The crossing of the river marks the departure from a patron who thought merit could be counted. The emperor is the believer who has built temples and expects credit.

section.label: Teaching
section.p: The case teaches the emptiness of holy things (kakunen musshō, 廓然無聖) and the refusal of merit as a reward. The wall-gazing is the origin of seated practice (zazen) in the lineage story, which later Zen retained.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A refusal to explain, deliberate withdrawal, or sustained effort without an audience. The card names solitude in the service of a long task.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Withdrawal as a pose, or the stubbornness that mistakes obstinacy for depth. The emperor's error, expecting reward for good works, has a counterpart in the practitioner who expects recognition for sitting.

section.label: Links
section.p: XI — The Flower and the Smile: the previous link in the legendary line. XIII — Pacifying the Mind: the disciple who arrives at the wall. XIV — No Mirror, No Stand: the later patriarch who also denies the holy.

description.p: A worry looked at directly, which loses its solid form.

section.label: Source
section.p: Mumonkan case 41, Wumen Huikai, 1228. The story of Huike's arm appears in earlier Chan histories in several variants and is generally regarded as legend.

section.label: Scene
section.p: Bodhidharma sits facing a wall. Huike stands in the snow, and in some versions cuts off his arm to prove his sincerity. He says that his mind is not at peace and asks Bodhidharma to pacify it. Bodhidharma says, "Bring me your mind, and I will pacify it." Huike answers that he has searched for it and cannot find it. Bodhidharma says, "Then it is already pacified." Wumen's commentary is critical of the whole performance, saying that the old foreigner caused trouble and the disciple made it worse by mutilating himself.

section.label: Symbols
section.p: The snow is the test of the seeker's resolve. The severed arm is the sacrifice offered, which in the commentary is excessive. The mind that cannot be found is the central image: the object of the search is not an object. Bodhidharma's turned back is the teaching that offers no reassurance.

section.label: Teaching
section.p: The doctrine is the emptiness of the mind as a thing (shin fukatoku, 心不可得), a theme from the Diamond Sutra: past, present and future mind cannot be grasped. Peace of mind (anjin, 安心) comes from looking directly at the troubled mind and finding no one there to be troubled.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Anxiety brought to a teacher, a friend or oneself, and the discovery that looking at it dissolves its solid form. The card can name the moment a persistent worry loses its object.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Treating the exchange as a trick and "not finding the mind" as a technique for dispelling distress. The other error is the arm: dramatic sacrifice as a substitute for looking.

section.label: Links
section.p: XII — Facing the Wall: the master who does not turn around. VII — The Ox Forgotten: the mind sought and the means abandoned. XIV — No Mirror, No Stand: a later denial of a mind to be cleaned.

description.p: Dropping a project of self-improvement whose problem does not exist.

section.label: Source
section.p: Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch, verse contest between Shenxiu and Huineng. The text is attributed to Fahai, a disciple of Huineng, but its authorship is disputed: the oldest manuscripts from Dunhuang date to the 9th century and derive from an edition of about 780, the text went through later editions (1056, 1291), and some scholars see a hand from the Oxhead school. The verse contest may be a later story. In the Dunhuang version Huineng's verse differs from the later and more famous wording of "originally there is not a thing", which is the version the card title follows.

section.label: Scene
section.p: The Fifth Patriarch Hongren asks his monks to write a verse showing their understanding; the author of the best will inherit robe and dharma. Shenxiu, the senior monk, writes anonymously on the corridor wall that the body is a bodhi tree and the mind a bright mirror on a stand, to be wiped constantly so that no dust settles. Huineng, an illiterate lay worker in the threshing room, has the verse read to him and dictates a reply: there is no bodhi tree and no mirror stand, and since there is nothing, dust has nowhere to land. Hongren secretly approves, publicly rubs out the verse, and later transmits the robe to Huineng by night.

section.label: Symbols
section.p: The mirror is the mind in its clear state. The dust is delusion and the cleaning is gradual practice. The tree is the body as the site of awakening. Huineng's reply removes mirror, stand and tree. The robe is the sign of transmission, and the night handover marks a lineage in danger.

section.label: Teaching
section.p: The two verses are the textbook pair for the "gradual" and "sudden" approaches (jian and dun), a reading of the Southern school, though modern scholars including John McRae argue Shenxiu's verse was not understood as gradualism in its own time. The doctrinal core is emptiness (śūnyatā) and the lack of an inherent self (anātman).

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Dropping a project of self-improvement, or recognising that the problem imagined as dirt on a surface does not exist. It can also name a talent from an unexpected quarter.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Taking Huineng's verse as permission to give up practice and cleaning, which is the objection raised against it in later centuries. A verse proving that there is nothing to clean can itself become something to cling to.

section.label: Links
section.p: XIII — Pacifying the Mind: the mind that cannot be found. VIII — The Ox and the Man Both Gone: the same emptiness in a different image. XII — Facing the Wall: the lineage's earlier denial of holiness.

description.p: Attention to what is already in front of you.

section.label: Source
section.p: Mumonkan case 19, Wumen Huikai, 1228. The exchange is between the Tang masters Nanquan Puyuan (Jp. Nansen) and his student Zhaozhou Congshen (Jp. Jōshū), before Zhaozhou became a teacher in his own right. The dialogue is a Chan record and has no particular claim to be a verbatim report.

section.label: Scene
section.p: Zhaozhou asks Nanquan what the Way is. Nanquan answers that ordinary mind is the Way. Zhaozhou asks whether he should direct himself toward it, and Nanquan says that if you try to direct yourself toward it, you turn away from it. Zhaozhou asks how he can know the Way without directing himself, and Nanquan says that the Way belongs neither to knowing nor to not knowing: knowing is delusion, and not knowing is blankness. If one truly reaches the Way beyond doubt, it is like vast space, open and empty, so how could there be right and wrong in it? At these words Zhaozhou is awakened. Wumen remarks that Zhaozhou still needed thirty years to digest it.

section.label: Symbols
section.p: The case has no props, and the card shows an ordinary setting on an unmarked day. Vast space stands for a mind without a centre from which to judge. The thirty years in Wumen's commentary mark the time that realisation takes to become habit.

section.label: Teaching
section.p: Heijōshin (平常心) is the mind of ordinary daily life, not a special state. The case rejects both the effort to produce a state and the complacency of having none. The teaching joins the Mahāyāna principle of non-duality with the Chinese preference for the everyday.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Attention to what is already in front of you: an ordinary meal, a task, a day. The card recommends dropping the project of becoming special, and it may mark the end of a search that was itself the obstacle.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Using "ordinary" as an excuse for carelessness or laziness, treating any behaviour as the Way. Nanquan's refusal of both knowing and not knowing leaves no resting place for this reading either.

section.label: Links
section.p: 0 — Mu: the same Zhaozhou, first as the student and then as the master of the dog. IX — Returning to the Source: the world as it is, seen after emptiness. XVI — The Wild Fox: ordinary mind still stands under cause and effect.

description.p: A loophole used once too often: no insight exempts one from consequences.

section.label: Source
section.p: Mumonkan case 2, Wumen Huikai, 1228. The setting is the monastery of the Tang master Baizhang Huaihai (Jp. Hyakujō); the story is a teaching narrative with no independent corroboration.

section.label: Scene
section.p: An old man who attends Baizhang's lectures tells him that he is not human. In the time of a former Buddha he was the abbot of the same mountain. Asked whether an enlightened person falls under the law of cause and effect, he answered that such a person does not, and for this he has been reborn as a fox for five hundred lives. He asks Baizhang the same question, and Baizhang replies that an enlightened person does not obscure cause and effect. The old man is freed at these words and asks for a monk's funeral. Baizhang holds the funeral, and after the meal leads the monks to a cave, where he finds the body of a fox. Huangbo then asks what would have happened had the old man answered correctly each time. Baizhang tells him to come closer, Huangbo slaps him, and Baizhang laughs. Wumen's commentary asks why a wrong answer produced a fox and a right answer released one, and says that anyone with the one eye will see.

section.label: Symbols
section.p: The fox is the cunning mind that has slipped into a doctrine and made it a licence. The cave is the place where the former self is buried. The funeral for an animal shows that the tradition honours the practitioner whatever his form. The slap and the laugh are an exchange between teacher and student.

section.label: Teaching
section.p: The case concerns inga (因果), cause and effect, and the Zen claim that awakening does not suspend karma. The old abbot's answer was "does not fall into" cause and effect (furaku inga, 不落因果); Baizhang's is "does not obscure" it (fumai inga, 不昧因果). Translators render 昧 as "obscure", "ignore" or "be blind to".

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A loophole used once too often: the belief that insight, status or intention exempts one from the consequences of one's acts. The card can also name a cost that has been carried a long time and is finally being released.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: The error it depicts: treating realisation as freedom from consequences. The opposite error is the fatalism that lets cause and effect crush any possibility of change.

section.label: Links
section.p: IV — Catching the Ox: the wildness of the unmastered mind. XIV — No Mirror, No Stand: emptiness stated without the reminder this card supplies. XV — Ordinary Mind: the ordinary life in which cause and effect operate.

description.p: A direct interruption that cuts off a borrowed story.

section.label: Source
section.p: Linji lu (Record of Linji), the passage known as the Four Shouts; Linji Yixuan (Jp. Rinzai, died 866). The standard text was compiled by Yuanjue Zongyan and printed in 1120, about 250 years after Linji's death, and Albert Welter has argued that later editors shaped it, so the passage is the tradition's record and not a transcript. Blue Cliff Record case 10 (Muzhou and a shouting monk, 1125) is a related case about an imitated shout.

section.label: Scene
section.p: In Burton Watson's translation, Linji asks a monk whether he understands the shout. At times, he says, it is like the precious sword of the Diamond King, at times like a golden-haired lion crouching on the ground, at times like the search pole and the shadow grass, and at times it does not work like a shout at all. When the monk hesitates to answer, Linji shouts. In the Blue Cliff case the old master Muzhou asks a monk where he has come from, and the monk shouts. Muzhou says he has been shouted at once. The monk shouts again, and Muzhou asks what comes after three or four shouts. The monk has no answer, and Muzhou strikes him and calls him a thieving phony. The Four Shouts passage was not checked against a printed translation; the account above rests on secondary reports of Watson's rendering.

section.label: Symbols
section.p: The shout (katsu, 喝) is a sound with no meaning, so it carries no concept. The sword cuts through, the lion presides, the pole and grass probe whether a visitor is genuine, and the fourth shout is the one that lacks the form of a shout. The strike that follows is a teacher's reply to a gesture that was imitated and not lived.

section.label: Teaching
section.p: Linji's teaching centres on the "true person of no rank" (mui no shinnin, 無位真人) who is already present in the body, and on the demand to depend on no external authority: "if you meet the Buddha, kill the Buddha" is the familiar form. The shout is the practice of cutting off conceptual replies. The fourfold structure is a way of testing students in encounter dialogue (mondō).

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A direct interruption, at the right or the wrong moment: a plain refusal of the story a person is telling. The card may name a candid word that breaks a cycle, or the reader's own need to be cut off from borrowed authority.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Imitation. The monk in case 10 shouts as a performance, and the teacher answers a copy with a stick. Loudness and aggression are not a Zen method. The later tradition warns against empty shouting and against the habit of dismissing others' views.

section.label: Links
section.p: XV — Ordinary Mind: the quiet pole of the same tradition. X — Entering the Market with Open Hands: gentle help, set against the sharp version here. 0 — Mu: another syllable that cuts rather than explains.

description.p: A search for stability that has not yet found its ground.

section.label: Stage
section.p: This is the first ox-herding stage in the domain of the body: the search for a place to sit. The seeker tries chairs, cushions, benches and postures, and expects one of them to bring the stillness he has read about.

section.label: Image
section.p: A round black cushion on a bare wooden floor in early grey light. A pair of straw sandals lies at the threshold, and a single sliding door stands open on a garden of wet moss.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Restlessness in the body, and the first decision to give it a place.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A search for stability that has not yet found its ground. The card marks a person who wants to settle and has not decided where. It suggests choosing one place and one hour.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Treating the search as research: comparing cushions, retreats and teachers while the sitting itself is postponed. Dōgen's Fukanzazengi asks for a quiet room and a seat.

section.label: Links
section.p: I — Searching for the Ox: the same restlessness, shown here as the body that will not stay still. Seven of Water: the settled feeling that this search is looking for.

description.p: Early signs that a discipline is within reach.

section.label: Stage
section.p: The seeker finds the traces of sitting. He reads an account of posture, notices a stiff knee after the first attempt, and sees a hollow in a cushion that someone else has used. These are signs that a practice exists and that bodies have settled before his.

section.label: Image
section.p: A well-worn cushion with a deep impression at its centre, and beside it an open manual with a drawing of crossed legs.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Evidence from outside and from the body that sitting works. The card names instruction, imitation and the first aches.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Early signs that a discipline is within reach. The card suggests following the instructions as written and noting what the body reports.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Mistaking knowledge of posture for the posture. A person can describe the angle of the spine, the position of the hands and the line of the gaze, and never sit for more than a minute.

section.label: Links
section.p: II — Seeing the Traces: the footprints here are a hollow in a cushion and a page of instructions. Two of Wind: the breath, which the manual mentions next.

description.p: A brief, real steadiness has appeared and should be kept without being inflated.

section.label: Stage
section.p: In the third stage the ox is seen directly. Here a sitting arrives in which the body settles of its own accord: the weight drops into the hips, the spine rises without effort, and the floor feels like a support. It lasts a few minutes.

section.label: Image
section.p: A figure seated in profile beside a window at dusk, shoulders level, hands resting in the lap. A square of last light lies across the knees.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: A first experience of stability that did not need to be made. The card names the moment when sitting stops being a task.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A brief, real steadiness has appeared and should be kept without being inflated. The card suggests returning to the cushion the next day as before.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Setting out to repeat the sitting, which makes the body tense in search of the memory. The settled posture arrives while attention is elsewhere.

section.label: Links
section.p: III — Seeing the Ox: a glimpse, here felt in the hips and spine. Four of Fire: the effort that must now hold what has been seen.

description.p: A resolve is being tested by routine.

section.label: Stage
section.p: The ox is caught by the discipline of keeping to the schedule. The seeker sits at the same hour each day, through cold mornings, sleepiness and the pain of the legs. Posture is held when the mind wants to shift, and the alarm is obeyed.

section.label: Image
section.p: A man seated before dawn in an unheated hall, breath visible, a lit stick of incense burned halfway down. His knees are bound by a cloth belt, and a lantern hangs at the door.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Firm commitment to the body's discipline. The card names regularity enforced against inclination.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A resolve is being tested by routine. The card calls for a fixed schedule kept without bargaining, in training, in work or in the care of the body. It favours endurance over variety.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Severity. Sitting through pain as a contest of will turns the cushion into a place of endurance, and the injured knee becomes a trophy. Dōgen describes zazen as the dharma gate of repose and bliss, which excludes grim effort.

section.label: Links
section.p: IV — Catching the Ox: the rope is a fixed hour and a fixed posture. Five of Earth: the same discipline once it has become routine.

description.p: Steady, ordinary progress made by regular habit.

section.label: Stage
section.p: The ox is herded by routine. Sitting, meals, cleaning and sleep follow one another in a fixed order, and the days take on a shape. The posture needs less force, but it still needs tending, and lapses are corrected when noticed.

section.label: Image
section.p: A temple corridor with a bucket, a rag and a row of shoes set neatly on a step. A monk kneels at one end, wiping the boards in long strokes, and the grain of the wood shows through the water.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Practice sustained by order. The card names the unglamorous middle of any work.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Steady, ordinary progress made by regular habit. The card favours maintenance, repetition and small repairs over any new start, and it suggests that the schedule is the achievement.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Rigidity. A routine can become the thing guarded, with the person anxious when it breaks and proud when it holds. The tether is meant to become unnecessary.

section.label: Links
section.p: V — Herding the Ox: the string and the whip are the daily schedule. Eight of Water: a looser form of the same attention, in the tea room.

description.p: Effort is rewarded with comfort, and the foundations are sound.

section.label: Stage
section.p: The seeker rides the ox home. Sitting no longer feels like work against the body, and the body returns the favour: sleep is sound, the back is straight and the legs have stopped complaining. The cushion is a familiar place rather than an assignment.

section.label: Image
section.p: A broad-shouldered monk seated under a pine in the evening, eyes half open, a flute lying across his lap. A path behind him leads down to a village with lit windows.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Ease in the body after a long discipline. The card names the comfort of a practice that has become habitual.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Effort is rewarded with comfort, and the foundations are sound. The card suggests enjoying the stability without examining it too closely. It can name a settled home, a healthy period or a skill that has become easy.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Contentment. The pleasant sitting becomes the purpose, and the cushion is visited for its comfort. The ox is still under the rider.

section.label: Links
section.p: VI — Riding the Ox Home: the ride is the body at ease in its posture. Three of Wind: the walk that follows a long sit.

description.p: A discipline has become part of the person and no longer needs watching.

section.label: Stage
section.p: The ox is forgotten and the man remains. The seeker puts down the rope: he stops counting breaths, stops checking his posture and stops measuring his sittings. The practice goes on in the body without supervision, in daily work as much as on the cushion.

section.label: Image
section.p: A thatched hut in morning light. A coil of rope hangs unused on a nail, and a man sits on the veranda with his back to the room, sipping from a bowl.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: A method has done its work and can be set down. The card names the end of self-monitoring.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A discipline has become part of the person and no longer needs watching. The card suggests that rules once kept by effort can be relaxed. It asks what remains when the scaffolding comes down.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Pride in having let go. The one who no longer checks still thinks of himself as the one who sits, and that image remains.

section.label: Links
section.p: VII — The Ox Forgotten, Leaving the Man Alone: the rope is dropped and the sitter stays. Six of Void: the awareness that does not need a posture.

description.p: A phase in which roles and ground alike seem to give way.

section.label: Stage
section.p: Man and ox are both gone. In sitting, there is no longer a sitter with a body to be placed. Dōgen's phrase shinjin datsuraku, the dropping off of body and mind, belongs to this stage, as the tradition tells it of his awakening under Rujing. The hall remains, and no one occupies it.

section.label: Image
section.p: An empty zendo at dawn with a single cushion in the centre, undented, and a wide circle of pale light on the floor where the sun enters. No figure appears.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Sitting without a subject. The card names the dissolving of the body as a possession.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A phase in which roles and ground alike seem to give way. The card can mean relief, loss of footing or a pause with no content.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Treating the quiet as the goal. Hakuin warned of the dead stillness, the cave of the black mountain, in which sitting goes on with no change in life.

section.label: Links
section.p: VIII — The Ox and the Man Both Gone Out of Sight: the empty circle, found here in the floor of the hall. One of Void: the awareness that remains in the absence.

description.p: Clear sight of an ordinary situation, with nothing to add.

section.label: Stage
section.p: The seeker returns to the source and finds the ground as it was. The floor is boards, the cushion is cloth, the body is flesh, and none of them needs to be made into anything. Sitting, sweeping and eating are seen as they are.

section.label: Image
section.p: A wooden floor, a window, a broom leaning on the wall, and a bowl on the sill. Beyond the glass a river runs through red maples. No person appears.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The plain world, seen after its dissolution. The card names things restored to themselves.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Clear sight of an ordinary situation, with nothing to add. The card suggests that a home, a body or a task already holds what was looked for elsewhere. It marks the return of confidence in what is near.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Quietism. The clear room is enjoyed and the world outside is left to itself. The sitter who has returned to the source is still asked to open the door.

section.label: Links
section.p: IX — Returning to the Source: the river and the maples are the water and flowers of that card. Nine of Wind: the speech that can now describe things as they are.

description.p: Practical service in an ordinary setting.

section.label: Stage
section.p: The seeker goes out among people with the settled body as his only tool. He cooks, carries, mends and digs. The sitting he does at home shows in the way he works: unhurried, attentive and fit for the task.

section.label: Image
section.p: A barefoot cook at a market stall, sleeves tied back, handing a bowl of rice to a labourer. A basket of radishes sits at his feet, and a child watches from under the awning.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Daily work done well, among others, with open hands. The card names usefulness without display.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Practical service in an ordinary setting. The card points to work in the household, a trade or a community, and to labour that needs no recognition. It also closes a round, and the next card begins the search again.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Ostentatious humility, or the holiness of someone who cleans in front of an audience. Dōgen's Tenzo kyōkun asks the cook to handle the rice and vegetables as his own eyes, which leaves no room for performance.

section.label: Links
section.p: X — Entering the Market with Open Hands: the market here is a kitchen and a street. Ten of Water: the same giving, in the tea room.

description.p: A withdrawn, composed person, or a period of retreat from ordinary affairs.

section.label: Rank
section.p: Shō chū hen (正中偏), the relative within the absolute. In the element of Earth it is the first sight of solid things as empty: the body, the floor and the mountain are seen to be without a fixed nature, and the mind lies down in that.

section.label: Figure
section.p: A recluse seated in a mountain hollow, eyes closed, wrapped in a grey robe. Moss has crept over his knees, and rock and sitter share one outline.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Emptiness realised first, in the stillness of the body. The card names a person for whom the world has gone quiet.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A withdrawn, composed person, or a period of retreat from ordinary affairs. The card gives credit for clarity and watches for the point where clarity stops.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Hakuin warned that this rank can become a trap, the dead sitting in the cave of the black mountain. The seat is comfortable, and the comfort keeps the sitter there.

section.label: Links
section.p: VIII — The Ox and the Man Both Gone Out of Sight: the emptiness that this figure has reached and settled in. IV — Catching the Ox: the discipline that brought him to the cushion and that he may no longer need to keep.

description.p: Careful attention to particulars, and the sense that each carries more than it seems.

section.label: Rank
section.p: Hen chū shō (偏中正), the absolute within the relative. In Earth it is the recognition of emptiness in solid particulars: the weight of a bowl, the grain of a table, the warmth of a floor in the sun.

section.label: Figure
section.p: A potter in a workshop, hands wet with clay, looking at a bowl on the wheel. Shelves of finished and unfinished work stand behind, each piece slightly different. The expression is attentive and calm.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The ultimate found in what is nearest. The card names a person who sees the whole in a single object.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Careful attention to particulars, and the sense that each carries more than it seems. The card favours craft, study of detail and respect for materials. It can name a person who teaches by the way things are made.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Aestheticism. Beauty found in a bowl becomes a taste to be cultivated, and the potter prizes his own perception above the clay.

section.label: Links
section.p: IX — Returning to the Source: the world seen as it is, in its particulars. II — Seeing the Traces: here the traces are the objects themselves.

description.p: Action taken from a stable position, with steadiness rather than force.

section.label: Rank
section.p: Shō chū rai (正中來), coming from within the absolute. In Earth, action arises from an emptiness that holds the body steady: the hands do what the work asks, and no self stands between the task and the doing.

section.label: Figure
section.p: A builder on a half-finished roof, fitting a beam, with scaffolding and tools laid in order around him. Below, villagers hold the ropes. He looks at the joint and not at the onlookers.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Work that comes out of stillness. The card names a person who acts without hesitation from a settled ground.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Action taken from a stable position, with steadiness rather than force. The card suggests that the moment for building has come and that the foundation is sufficient. It can name a competent organiser or a calm presence in a crisis.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Tireless doing. The builder who cannot stop has mistaken productivity for the ground it came from, and the stillness is used up.

section.label: Links
section.p: X — Entering the Market with Open Hands: action for others that costs the actor nothing. V — Herding the Ox: the discipline now so well absorbed that it is invisible.

description.p: A balanced life in which the foundation and the daily tasks agree.

section.label: Rank
section.p: Ken chū shi (兼中至), arriving at mutual integration. In Earth the sitter and the worker are one: the cushion and the field, the stillness and the labour are two sides of a single practice and each supports the other.

section.label: Figure
section.p: A farmer with a hoe on his shoulder, walking home from the field at dusk, sitting for a moment on a stump at the edge of the path. Behind him the rows run straight to the horizon.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Engagement with the world on both sides of the practice. The card names a person for whom sitting and working inform one another.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A balanced life in which the foundation and the daily tasks agree. The card suggests that nothing needs to be given up in order to keep the other.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Self-satisfaction with the balance. A well-arranged life can be held up as a model, and the arrangement then becomes one more thing to protect.

section.label: Links
section.p: XV — Ordinary Mind: the plain manner in which the two sides cooperate. VI — Riding the Ox Home: the earlier ease, now shared with the world.

description.p: Maturity that has no need to be noticed.

section.label: Rank
section.p: Ken chū tō (兼中到), unity attained. In Earth it is a person who leaves no trace of sitting or of work. The body is ordinary, the day is ordinary, and nothing in the manner suggests practice or its result.

section.label: Figure
section.p: An old woman sweeping a yard in the early morning, with a straw broom and a bent back. Fallen leaves lie in small heaps.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Completion without display. The card names a person whose attainment cannot be told from daily life.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Maturity that has no need to be noticed. The card suggests that the best course is the plain one already under way, and that a quiet person may be the most settled in the room.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Pursuing the absence of a trace as a style. A cultivated plainness is itself a mark, and the tradition's phrase for it is the stench of Zen.

section.label: Links
section.p: X — Entering the Market with Open Hands: the sweeper and the figure in the market are one. 0 — Mu: the question that began the practice and has no further need to be asked.

description.p: An unnamed longing is moving things along.

section.label: Stage
section.p: Searching for the Ox, played out in feeling. A restlessness with no named object: a thirst that tea, company and conversation each fail to settle. The person moves from one relationship or mood to the next, sure that the missing thing is in the next one.

section.label: Image
section.p: A tea bowl stands empty on a wooden veranda in light rain. Beyond it a path runs down through mist toward a river, and no figure is visible.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Longing before it knows its object. The card names the dissatisfaction that sends a person out, and the habit of taking each new feeling for an answer.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: An unnamed longing is moving things along. The card marks a time when company and comfort fail to satisfy, and it asks what is actually being looked for. The feeling is the beginning of a path, and it needs no immediate cure.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Chasing sensation: a new friend, a new grief, a new intensity each season, each treated as the thing itself. The opposite error is to numb the thirst so that no search starts.

section.label: Links
section.p: I — Searching for the Ox: the same restless seeker, here in the medium of feeling. 0 — Mu: the question under the longing, which no person or mood answers.

description.p: Signs of a real bond are appearing before the bond is felt.

section.label: Stage
section.p: Seeing the Traces, in the domain of relationship. Evidence appears that something real lies under the moods: a letter kept for years, a friend whose manner steadies a room, a ring left by a cup on the table. The person reads these signs but has not yet felt the thing they point to.

section.label: Image
section.p: Wet footprints cross a dry stone step and lead into a tea room. A single ripple is spreading across a stone basin in the garden outside.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Early signs of connection. The card names what is learned about feeling from accounts, examples and the traces left by other people.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Signs of a real bond are appearing before the bond is felt. The card suggests following them, and it warns that a description of intimacy is not intimacy. A period of reading, listening and observation is indicated.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Treating knowledge about feeling as feeling: fluent talk about empathy, attachment and boundaries from someone who has not yet sat across from another person without a script.

section.label: Links
section.p: II — Seeing the Traces: the footprints in the stream, here left by other people. VI — Riding the Ox Home: the ease that these first signs will eventually lead to.

description.p: A moment of unguarded contact has shown what is possible.

section.label: Stage
section.p: Seeing the Ox, in the stream of feeling. For a moment contact is direct: a glance across a room, a bowl of tea drunk in silence with a stranger, grief that for once carries no story. The separation between the one who feels and what is felt thins.

section.label: Image
section.p: Moonlight lies in a bowl of still water on a low table. A hand hovers above it, and the surface is unbroken.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Immediacy in feeling. The card names the first time a feeling is met as it is, with no commentary running beside it.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A moment of unguarded contact has shown what is possible. The card says the moment was real and gives no promise that it will return. It is best held loosely and not retold.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Grasping the moment: trying to reproduce the exact conditions, or announcing the experience to friends so that it hardens into an identity. Water taken up in a closed hand runs out.

section.label: Links
section.p: III — Seeing the Ox: the first direct sight, here arriving through the heart. IV — Catching the Ox: the effort that follows once the glimpse has gone.

description.p: A strong feeling is demanding steady attention.

section.label: Stage
section.p: Catching the Ox, as the work of holding a strong feeling. Anger, grief or desire arrives with force, and the person must stay with it without being thrown. Attention is the rope, and the feeling pulls hard against it.

section.label: Image
section.p: A figure carries a full bowl across a wooden bridge in wind, both hands under it, knees bent. Water trembles at the rim and does not spill.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The effort of staying present with strong emotion. The card names the stage at which feeling is neither indulged nor pushed away but held.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A strong feeling is demanding steady attention. The card calls for some firmness and for staying in the room. It also notes that old reactions return quickly, and that patience with them is part of the work.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Gripping too hard. Suppression passes for discipline, and the bowl is clutched so tightly that nothing can move through it. The other error is to let the bowl drop at the first spill.

section.label: Links
section.p: IV — Catching the Ox: the same struggle with a wild animal, here fought in the heart. XVI — The Wild Fox: the feeling that claims to be free of consequences.

description.p: Regular, quiet attention is what the situation needs.

section.label: Stage
section.p: Herding the Ox, as the daily care of relationship. The crisis has passed and what remains is upkeep: the call made on schedule, the apology offered early, the tea prepared with the same attention on an ordinary Tuesday. Rikyū's rules for tea begin with making a good bowl and laying the charcoal so that it heats the water, which is the same kind of unglamorous order.

section.label: Image
section.p: A channel of water runs through a garden between two lines of stones. A figure kneels and clears a fallen leaf from the gate where it enters.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Steady attention that keeps a bond flowing. The card names regularity as the form care takes between people.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Regular, quiet attention is what the situation needs. The card favours routine over gesture, and it counsels patience while habits settle into a pattern.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Making the routine the purpose. Rituals of courtesy become a performance of care, and the channel is cleared so often that no one remembers where the water goes.

section.label: Links
section.p: V — Herding the Ox: the nose-string and the whip, here shown as small daily courtesies. XV — Ordinary Mind: the point at which such care no longer feels like effort.

description.p: A relationship or a way of feeling has settled into ease.

section.label: Stage
section.p: Riding the Ox Home, in ease with others. Feeling and practice agree. Company no longer needs managing, and a long conversation with an old friend can wander without any one trying to steer it. Gain and loss in the relationship have stopped being the measure.

section.label: Image
section.p: Two people drift in a small boat on a wide river at dusk. One plays a bamboo flute and the other trails a hand in the water. The far bank is a faint line.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Harmony after effort. The card names the easy exchange between people who have done the work of understanding one another.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A relationship or a way of feeling has settled into ease. The card suggests that the work has been absorbed, and it invites enjoying the company without examining it.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Taking comfort for completion. The pleasant current carries the boat, and the passengers come to prefer it to any further question. Agreeableness can shelter a good deal of avoidance.

section.label: Links
section.p: VI — Riding the Ox Home: the flute, the evening and the lowered whip, here shared by two. XIV — No Mirror, No Stand: the ease of a mind that has stopped polishing itself.

description.p: A discipline, role or way of relating has become unnecessary and can be put down.

section.label: Stage
section.p: The Ox Forgotten, Leaving the Man Alone, in the tea way. The forms that once held a person steady, the ordered movements of preparing tea and the rules of etiquette, are no longer attended to. Tea is made without thought of procedure. The host remains, and with him the pleasure of being a good host.

section.label: Image
section.p: A tea room late in the afternoon. The utensils lie at rest on the tatami, and a single figure sits looking at the kettle. The door stands open to the garden.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The method has done its work. The card names the stage at which a form is released while the one who practised it stays.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A discipline, role or way of relating has become unnecessary and can be put down. The card asks what remains of the person once the scaffolding goes, and it advises resting before asking.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Pride in having let go. The host who no longer thinks of procedure comes to admire his own naturalness, and the self-regard takes the place of the old rules.

section.label: Links
section.p: VII — The Ox Forgotten: the means set aside. VIII — The Ox and the Man Both Gone Out of Sight: the host who will be dropped next.

description.p: Roles and attachments have lost their grip, and the situation has no clear form yet.

section.label: Stage
section.p: The Ox and the Man Both Gone Out of Sight, in feeling and relationship. Host and guest, giver and receiver, and the one who feels and what is felt, drop away together. A moment of grief or love arises with no owner to claim it.

section.label: Image
section.p: A plain bowl sits in the centre of an empty tatami room. A circular ring of damp, left by the bowl, is the only mark on the floor. The paper screens are closed and the light is even.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Feeling without a subject. The card names a clearing in which the roles through which relationships are held loosen.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Roles and attachments have lost their grip, and the situation has no clear form yet. The card can mean relief, numbness or a pause before a new arrangement. It asks that the quiet be allowed to stand for a time.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Settling into the cold. Detachment passes for peace, the heart is left like a dry well, and nothing in daily life changes. Hakuin's warning about the cave of the black mountain applies to the feelings as much as to the mind.

section.label: Links
section.p: VIII — The Ox and the Man Both Gone Out of Sight: the empty circle, here as an empty bowl. 0 — Mu: the blank under all the relationships.

description.p: A situation can be seen as it is, with nothing to add.

section.label: Stage
section.p: Returning to the Source, in perception. Water is seen as water. The kettle's hiss, the steam, the steadiness of the bowl are met without the commentary that once accompanied them. Feeling goes on in the same ordinary way that rivers run.

section.label: Image
section.p: An iron kettle simmers on a charcoal hearth in an empty tea room. Through the open shoji a stream runs past red maples. Neither the room nor the garden holds a figure.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Clear perception of the ordinary. The card names what the emptiness of the preceding stage gives back: a world of cups, kettles and friends, seen as they are.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A situation can be seen as it is, with nothing to add. The card suggests that the confusion has cleared and invites attention to what is already present. It also marks that nothing needs doing yet.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Quietism. The observer sits by the stream admiring the clarity and lets others pour their own tea. The verse of the ninth picture mocks the idea that returning is an achievement, and the same applies to admiring it.

section.label: Links
section.p: IX — Returning to the Source: the river flowing of its own accord. XV — Ordinary Mind: the plain world recovered in a master's words.

description.p: Generosity is called for, in the form of hospitality, listening or simple presence.

section.label: Stage
section.p: Entering the Market with Open Hands, in service. The practised steadiness of feeling is offered to strangers without announcement. A bowl of tea is handed to a traveller. A grief is shared without advice. The hands hang open, as the Chinese title of the picture suggests.

section.label: Image
section.p: A roadside stall under a straw awning. A barefoot man ladles water from a wooden bucket into a bowl for a weary porter, and others wait their turn. Children play in the puddle at the stall's edge.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Care for others that leaves no mark of distinction. The card names the stage at which feeling is put to use among people.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Generosity is called for, in the form of hospitality, listening or simple presence. The card also closes a cycle, and the next to be drawn is a beginning. Whatever was gained is for use.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Performing humility, or pouring from above. The helper who keeps count of what he gives has made a market of the gift. Rikyū's last rule, to treat everyone present with every consideration, is a check on this.

section.label: Links
section.p: X — Entering the Market with Open Hands: the same open-handed figure, here with a bucket of water. I — Searching for the Ox: the cycle begins again, with the old thirst met more lightly.

description.p: Emotional detachment, which is real but incomplete.

section.label: Rank
section.p: 正中偏 (shōchūhen), the relative within the absolute. In Water it is the emptiness of feeling seen first: all moods and attachments are recognised as passing, and the water is still.

section.label: Figure
section.p: A hermit of middle age who has seen through the surface of his own sorrows and joys. He sits beside a mountain pool in late autumn. The water is clear and no leaf moves on it.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Stillness reached by seeing that feelings have no fixed ground. The card shows a real insight that has not yet entered the life of the person.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Emotional detachment, which is real but incomplete. The card describes someone who has stopped being carried away and may be mistaking that for the end of the matter. It asks whether the stillness has a use.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Hakuin's warning about the first rank: stagnant water. The pool never moves, and the person comes to prefer its calm to the company of anyone whose feelings are not yet seen through. The detachment becomes a quiet form of coldness.

section.label: Links
section.p: VIII — The Ox and the Man Both Gone Out of Sight: the emptiness that the figure has tasted and holds as home. 0 — Mu: the blank he rests in, without yet asking it anything.

description.p: The extraordinary is being met in the ordinary.

section.label: Rank
section.p: 偏中正 (henchūshō), the absolute within the relative. In Water it means recognising the whole in the particular: a single bowl of tea contains the emptiness that the hermit saw in the mountains.

section.label: Figure
section.p: A tea host in middle life. He cleans a worn bowl with a white cloth in a small room, and the light from the window falls on the steam. His attention rests wholly on the bowl.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Emptiness found in ordinary things. The card shows a person for whom the insight of the first rank has come down into the objects of daily use.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: The extraordinary is being met in the ordinary. The card points to a person or time in which small tasks, meetings and exchanges carry unusual weight, with no need for a separate retreat.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Aestheticism. The bowl becomes the object of devotion and the host a connoisseur of his own refinement. Attention to particulars slides into collecting them.

section.label: Links
section.p: IX — Returning to the Source: mountains are mountains again, and tea is tea. XV — Ordinary Mind: the plain manner in which the particular carries the whole.

description.p: A response is being asked for, and it will be right if it comes without deliberation.

section.label: Rank
section.p: 正中來 (shōchūrai), coming from within the absolute. In Water, action and compassion arise from emptiness without a prior plan. Response to another person is quick and unrehearsed.

section.label: Figure
section.p: A ferryman at a river crossing. A traveller arrives at dusk in a hurry, and the ferryman is already holding the pole. His face shows no calculation. The boat is small and the current is strong.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Spontaneous help rooted in stillness. The card names the person whose adaptation to others has no residue of self-interest to slow it down.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A response is being asked for, and it will be right if it comes without deliberation. The card favours yielding to circumstance, as water takes the shape of the vessel. The Daodejing compares the highest good to water for this reason.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Mistaking reactivity for compassion. A person who yields to every pressure may be following habit and calling it flow, and the ferryman's calm is a result of long training.

section.label: Links
section.p: X — Entering the Market with Open Hands: action coming from emptiness. XVII — The Shout: another form of spontaneous response, in which the answer is given with force.

description.p: The situation holds both depth and ease, and two parties are well matched.

section.label: Rank
section.p: 兼中至 (kenchūshi), arriving at mutual integration. In Water the two sides, emptiness and form, stillness and feeling, work together. Each supports the other in the manner of host and guest.

section.label: Figure
section.p: A tea master and a guest kneel across a hearth, and it is difficult to say which is serving. Steam rises between them from a single bowl. The room is plain and warm.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Full engagement with others and with one's own feeling, while the ground of emptiness stays present. The card names the maturity of relationship.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: The situation holds both depth and ease, and two parties are well matched. The card suggests that nothing needs to be resolved between them. It favours conversation, collaboration and shared work.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Fixing the arrangement. Harmony between host and guest hardens into a ritual that excludes the unexpected visitor, and the integration becomes a style.

section.label: Links
section.p: XV — Ordinary Mind: everyday conduct as the way itself. XI — The Flower and the Smile: a meeting in which the whole is passed without explanation.

description.p: The matter resolves in plain conduct, without a sign of resolution.

section.label: Rank
section.p: 兼中到 (kenchūtō), unity attained. In Water the wholeness is mature and carries no trace of attainment. The person is indistinguishable from the common run of people drawing water from a well.

section.label: Figure
section.p: An old woman at a village well in the early morning, lowering a wooden bucket. She nods to a neighbour and goes on. Nothing in her manner or dress marks her out.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Ordinary life with the work of practice finished and unremarked. The card names a person in whom feeling, stillness and service are one thing.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: The matter resolves in plain conduct, without a sign of resolution. The card suggests that the question may be one that has stopped being asked. It is the quietest card in the suit.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Looking for the attainment. Seekers who expect a sage will walk past the well, and a reader who expects a sign will find the card empty. Imitating the plainness is a further form of display.

section.label: Links
section.p: X — Entering the Market with Open Hands: the unmarked figure among ordinary people. VIII — The Ox and the Man Both Gone Out of Sight: the emptiness that is now carried without being mentioned.

description.p: Energy is present and has not yet found its question.

section.label: Stage
