section.p: Searching for the Ox in the domain of effort. A restless energy has no direction yet: a monk or lay student feels a need to strive and tries one discipline after another, from fasting to long retreats to a heap of manuals.

section.label: Image
section.p: A lone figure in a dark hall holds a single lit taper and walks between pillars, the flame bending in the draught. The pillars fade into grey wash, and only the flame is tinted.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Will before its object. The heat is real, and what it should be spent on is undecided.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Energy is present and has not yet found its question. The card marks the start of a project or practice driven by restlessness more than by a plan. It asks what the effort is for before more of it is spent.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Treating intensity as progress. The student who adds harder methods each month is still searching, with more fuel.

section.label: Links
section.p: I — Searching for the Ox: the same seeker, now with a flame in hand instead of a road under foot. 0 — Mu: the question that will eventually give the fire something to burn.

description.p: Someone else's recorded struggle sheds light on the present one.

section.label: Stage
section.p: Seeing the Traces in the domain of koan work. The student reads the recorded cases and the commentaries on them, and finds that the old masters describe the same difficulty he is having.

section.label: Image
section.p: Two small braziers on a wooden floor, one burning and one holding grey ash with a faint line of smoke still rising. Beside them lies an open scroll, with no characters drawn.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Evidence that others have burned here before. The ash shows that the fire has been tended and that it can be read.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Someone else's recorded struggle sheds light on the present one. The card points to study, a teacher's remark or a case that clarifies the doubt. It advises reading with attention and without taking the commentary for the fire.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Becoming a connoisseur of koans: knowing the cases, their verses and their lineages while the question remains a topic and has not become a doubt.

section.label: Links
section.p: II — Seeing the Traces: the footprints are the cases, which point to the ox without being it. XI — The Flower and the Smile: the teaching that passes outside the scriptures, which the study here cannot supply.

description.p: A question has become impossible to put down.

section.label: Stage
section.p: Seeing the Ox in the domain of the great doubt. After weeks on a single head phrase, the question stops being something held and becomes something that holds. For a moment the doubt is whole.

section.label: Image
section.p: A red-hot iron ball rests on an anvil in a smithy, its glow lighting a bare forge and the hands of a smith. The room is otherwise grey ink, with the ball as the single warm shape.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The doubt at full heat. Mumon's image of the hot iron ball that cannot be swallowed or spat out describes it.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A question has become impossible to put down. The card marks a moment of concentrated attention in which the usual defences fall away. It asks that the heat be kept and not explained.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Mistaking the intensity for the answer, or announcing it. The glow passes, and the work of keeping the doubt alive remains.

section.label: Links
section.p: III — Seeing the Ox: a first direct sight, here reached through doubt. 0 — Mu: the head phrase on which this heat is raised.

description.p: A commitment that must be kept up when it has stopped being exciting.

section.label: Stage
section.p: Catching the Ox in the domain of will. The student has to hold the doubt through sleepiness, pain and boredom, with the sitting schedule as the rope and the keisaku as the whip.

section.label: Image
section.p: A figure kneels on a cushion, gripping a long stick across the lap while a flame burns steadily in a lamp ahead. Behind, a second shadow lifts the stick as if to strike a shoulder.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Discipline applied against the pull of old habit. Effort is the working part of the stage.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A commitment that must be kept up when it has stopped being exciting. The card recommends structure, regular hours and a companion who can notice drift. It reads as a time for steady effort and little invention.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Willing the practice as a fight with the self. Gripping harder tires the one who grips, and the ox pulls the other way.

section.label: Links
section.p: IV — Catching the Ox: the rope and the whip, here as schedule and stick. XVII — The Shout: a sharp interruption that can break the drowse.

description.p: The work has settled into a rhythm that needs tending more than inspiring.

section.label: Stage
section.p: Herding the Ox in the domain of daily effort. The doubt is no longer a crisis, and it has to be carried through ordinary tasks: sweeping, cooking, answering letters. The flame is lowered to a level that can last.

section.label: Image
section.p: A kitchen hearth at dusk, a small controlled fire under a kettle, and a monk crouching to lay a split log with care. A string of dried radishes hangs above in grey wash.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Fire kept alive without being fed more than it needs. Steady attention replaces the earlier bursts.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: The work has settled into a rhythm that needs tending more than inspiring. The card suggests that consistency now matters more than intensity. It points to the unglamorous middle of a long undertaking.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Letting the fire go out through neglect, or building it up again in search of the old drama. Either error ends the habit that was forming.

section.label: Links
section.p: V — Herding the Ox: the ox follows when the rope is slack, and the hearth burns when the log is laid. XII — Facing the Wall: long uneventful sitting.

description.p: Hard work has paid off and the effort now feels natural.

section.label: Stage
section.p: Riding the Ox Home in the domain of koan work. The case that took years has come through, and the student carries it with ease, answering the teacher in the room without strain.

section.label: Image
section.p: A figure walks a lantern-lit path at dusk, carrying a lit paper lantern at the end of a pole. The flame is steady and the walker looks at the ground ahead, relaxed.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Effort that has become easy. The fire gives light and little struggle.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Hard work has paid off and the effort now feels natural. The card marks competence that no longer needs to be proved. It advises enjoying the ease without turning it into a position.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Believing the work finished. Hakuin held that passing a koan is the start of deeper practice, and the student who rests here is easily drawn into complacency.

section.label: Links
section.p: VI — Riding the Ox Home: the same ease, the flute replaced by a lantern. III — Seeing the Ox: the sight that this steadiness grew from.

description.p: A technique, goal or ambition that once drove the work has lost its hold.

section.label: Stage
section.p: The Ox Forgotten, Leaving the Man Alone, in the domain of effort. The device that carried the practice, the head phrase or the counting of will, drops away, and only the person remains, still working.

section.label: Image
section.p: An empty tripod stands on a cold hearth in a bare room, with a few embers glowing beneath the ash. Through the open door, a figure sits in sunlight on the veranda.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Will without a tool. The method has served and been set down.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A technique, goal or ambition that once drove the work has lost its hold. The card says this loss is a stage and not a failure. It invites a pause before any new device is picked up.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Taking the quiet for laziness and reaching for a new method, or taking it for attainment and settling there.

section.label: Links
section.p: VII — The Ox Forgotten, Leaving the Man Alone: the rope and ox are gone, the person remains. XV — Ordinary Mind: the effort that dissolves into the plain day.

description.p: The drive that carried a long effort has ended, and nothing has replaced it yet.

section.label: Stage
section.p: The Ox and the Man Both Gone Out of Sight, in the domain of the great doubt. Both the question and the questioner fall away, and the doubt, which seemed the engine of the practice, has burned itself out.

section.label: Image
section.p: A bare hearth with a ring of white ash and no flame, drawn as an empty circle on blank paper. A thin grey thread of smoke leaves the centre and dissolves.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Fire after its fuel is spent. What remains is a clearing, and the heat has gone with the one who felt it.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: The drive that carried a long effort has ended, and nothing has replaced it yet. The card names the gap and recommends not filling it quickly. It can mark the end of an obsession.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Mistaking the clearing for a void to be defended, or for depression to be cured. Both readings add a story to what has been left bare.

section.label: Links
section.p: VIII — The Ox and the Man Both Gone Out of Sight: the empty circle. 0 — Mu: the question that could not be answered has ceased to need an answer.

description.p: The result arrives without being forced, and the work looks different in retrospect.

section.label: Stage
section.p: Returning to the Source in the domain of effort. Fire is seen as a natural process, like a pine in the wind or the sun on a ridge. The student finds that the work was always part of the world's own burning.

section.label: Image
section.p: A mountain stream under a rising sun, with fresh red maples on the bank in a faint wash of colour. A single burnt stump in the foreground sprouts a green shoot.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Warmth that needs no effort to maintain. The sun and the leaves do the work that the student once thought was theirs.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: The result arrives without being forced, and the work looks different in retrospect. The card marks a time of simple warmth and clear seeing. It suggests letting things ripen on their own schedule.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Concluding that effort was unnecessary. The ease of this stage rests on the earlier labour, and denying that is a way of misreading it.

section.label: Links
section.p: IX — Returning to the Source: the stream and the flowers go on as they were. XIII — Pacifying the Mind: the unrest that has stopped being a problem.

description.p: Skill and drive are being put to ordinary use among other people.

section.label: Stage
section.p: Entering the Market with Open Hands in the domain of will. The seasoned practitioner uses the energy of the work in the service of others: cooking, building, teaching, mending, with no display.

section.label: Image
section.p: A village street at night, with a charcoal seller's brazier glowing at a corner. A stranger in a worn robe warms both open palms over it beside a labourer and a child.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Warmth shared. The fire that once consumed its owner now heats the street.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Skill and drive are being put to ordinary use among other people. The card marks a time when the work is for the benefit of others and is done lightly. It also marks the return to a new beginning.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Burning out in service, or taking pride in giving. Either keeps the account open.

section.label: Links
section.p: X — Entering the Market with Open Hands: the open palms of this card, here held to a brazier. I — Searching for the Ox: the cycle returns, and the new search starts with a steadier flame.

description.p: A person who has seen that striving has no owner and may therefore stop striving.

section.label: Rank
section.p: 正中偏 (shō chū hen), the relative within the absolute. In Fire, this is the student who has been burned through by the great doubt and sees that no self stood behind the effort. All that was striven for is empty, and the person tends to stop there.

section.label: Figure
section.p: A seated monk beside a dead fire, hands in the sleeves of a robe, face turned from the flame. The ashes are grey, and the single touch of colour is a cooled ember at the foot.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Clarity about emptiness, with a draw toward rest. The fire has been seen through and has gone cold.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A person who has seen that striving has no owner and may therefore stop striving. The card advises respect for the insight and caution about the stillness that follows it. It asks whether withdrawal is wisdom or fatigue.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Hakuin warned that this is where many are trapped. He called such quiet the demon cave of the Black Mountain, in which the insight is held and nothing further is asked of it.

section.label: Links
section.p: VIII — The Ox and the Man Both Gone Out of Sight: the clearing that this person has reached and may not leave. XII — Facing the Wall: a stillness that can deepen or harden.

description.p: Meaning is found in a concrete task and not in a theory about it.

section.label: Rank
section.p: 偏中正 (hen chū shō), the absolute within the relative. In Fire, this is the person who finds the whole matter present in an ordinary flame: a match struck, a stove lit, charcoal glowing in a brazier.

section.label: Figure
section.p: A cook in an apron, crouched at a stove, with his face lit by a small fire. Behind, utensils hang on the wall in loose ink. The flame alone carries colour.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The empty and the particular seen together. Heat in the kettle is also heat in the sun.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Meaning is found in a concrete task and not in a theory about it. The card points to craft, to attention given to small jobs and to the value of familiar acts. It suggests that the matter being looked for is already at hand.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Turning the observation into a sentiment. A person who says that everything is sacred and then leaves the dishes has missed the point of the stove.

section.label: Links
section.p: III — Seeing the Ox: the ox appears in the particular scene. XV — Ordinary Mind: the plain way of lighting a fire is the way.

description.p: Decisive action that is not driven by fear or ambition.

section.label: Rank
section.p: 正中來 (shō chū rai), coming from within the absolute. In Fire, action arises from emptiness: vigorous, timely and without a plan. This is the teacher or worker whose energy comes without a motive attached.

section.label: Figure
section.p: A blacksmith or a teacher at the moment of striking, with sparks leaving the anvil in a clean arc. The face is calm and the arm is loose. The sparks are the only coloured marks.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Effort that begins from nowhere in particular and meets the situation as it is. The heat is an expression and not a store.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Decisive action that is not driven by fear or ambition. The card suggests that the moment for intervening has come and that the response will fit if it is not rehearsed. It can name a teacher who acts directly.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Confusing spontaneity with impulse. Action from emptiness has been prepared by long training, and an untrained burst is only temper.

section.label: Links
section.p: XVII — The Shout: a response that leaves no room for a second thought. XIV — No Mirror, No Stand: nothing is fixed in advance to guide it.

description.p: A person fully engaged in a difficult task without strain.

section.label: Rank
section.p: 兼中至 (ken chū shi), arriving at mutual integration. In Fire, will and release work together: the person is fully engaged in demanding work and equally free of it, and neither side leads.

section.label: Figure
section.p: A woman at a pottery kiln, tending the firebox with a long iron rake while a child hands her wood. Smoke rises into a pale sky. A thin line of red marks the firebox glow.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Hard work and ease at once. The heat is used, and nobody is consumed by it.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A person fully engaged in a difficult task without strain. The card marks a period of competence and shared labour where both determination and flexibility are called for. It suggests leaving the hands busy and the mind open.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Overwork under the heading of integration. Engagement that has no rest in it has dropped one of the two sides.

section.label: Links
section.p: V — Herding the Ox: care for the fire over a long time. X — Entering the Market with Open Hands: the work done among others.

description.p: Long effort that has become indistinguishable from life.

section.label: Rank
section.p: 兼中到 (ken chū tō), unity attained. In Fire, the effort of a lifetime shows as ordinary warmth. The person burns nothing and makes no mention of having done any of it.

section.label: Figure
section.p: An old woman sweeping a temple yard in the evening, a small bonfire of fallen leaves glowing beside her. The smoke drifts up in a thin grey line. Only the fire is in colour.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Maturity in which the work and the worker cannot be separated. The fire is lit when it is needed and left when it is not.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Long effort that has become indistinguishable from life. The card marks a person whose presence is useful without being noticed. It advises ordinary work and no announcement of results.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Trying to look the part. A show of simplicity is another form of display, and the fifth rank leaves no trace to show.

section.label: Links
section.p: IX — Returning to the Source: warmth as part of the landscape. XV — Ordinary Mind: the unremarkable way in which it is done.

description.p: A mind that will not settle on a single thing.

section.label: Stage
section.p: Searching for the Ox, played out in the breath. A person sits down to count breaths, and the mind leaves the count within a few exhalations. Each return to the count is followed by another departure, and the seeker has no sense yet of what is being sought.

section.label: Image
section.p: A figure sits on a cushion at dusk beside an open door. A few strokes of loose brush show the breath rising as a thin vapour, which frays and drifts toward the trees outside. No face is visible.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Restlessness at the first attempt to attend to something as plain as breathing. The card names the discovery that the mind does not stay where it is put.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A mind that will not settle on a single thing. The card describes scattered attention at the start of a task, a conversation or a practice, and it asks for a return to the count each time without keeping score. Failure at this stage is the material of the practice.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Treating the wandering as proof of unsuitability, or changing method at every lapse in the hope that a better technique will stop it.

section.label: Links
section.p: I — Searching for the Ox: the same restless seeker, here at the scale of one breath. 0 — Mu: the question that remains when counting fails.

description.p: Signs have appeared, and they are worth following.

section.label: Stage
section.p: Seeing the Traces, in the breath. The sitter begins to notice small signs: the cool of air at the nostrils, the slight rise of the belly, a pause at the end of the exhalation. These are reports about the breath and are not yet the breath itself.

section.label: Image
section.p: A hand held open before a paper window where a lantern flame leans and recovers. Beyond the paper, faint shadows of bamboo sway. The picture shows evidence of moving air and nothing of the air.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The first reliable indications that something can be attended to. The card names instruction, description and early observation.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Signs have appeared, and they are worth following. The card suggests reading what a teacher, a manual or a first experience has said and testing it against direct observation. A description of the breath is useful for as long as it sends the sitter back to breathing.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Collecting accounts of breathing, its physiology and its schools, and mistaking fluency about the subject for acquaintance with it.

section.label: Links
section.p: II — Seeing the Traces: the signs point to the ox without being the ox. XI — The Flower and the Smile: a transmission that does not go through description.

description.p: One moment of unmistakable presence has occurred.

section.label: Stage
section.p: Seeing the Ox, in the breath. For the length of a single inhalation and exhalation the sitter is wholly present, and the breath is seen as it is. The experience is brief, and it is clear that it was always available.

section.label: Image
section.p: A bare branch on a winter morning, a single leaf turning on its stalk in a gust. Mountains behind it are left as blank paper. The leaf is drawn in precise detail and the rest in pale wash.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: One complete breath, with nothing added. The card names the first direct taste of attention that is neither effort nor drift.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: One moment of unmistakable presence has occurred. The card says the moment was real and that its occurrence does not depend on a particular technique. It advises keeping the memory light and not building a story about it.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Chasing the moment: trying to reproduce the exact quality of that breath, which ensures that it does not return. A second error is reporting it to others as an achievement.

section.label: Links
section.p: III — Seeing the Ox: the glimpse of what was never absent. IV — Catching the Ox: the breath must now be held across many cycles.

description.p: A demanding stretch in which something must be held against resistance.

section.label: Stage
section.p: Catching the Ox, in the breath. The sitter counts from one to ten and begins again, and each lapse sends the count back to one. The effort is considerable. Attention is held by will, and the breath resists being observed without being managed.

section.label: Image
section.p: A figure walks into a hard crosswind along a ridge, robe pressed flat against the body, one hand clutching a hat. Grasses lie almost horizontal. The walker leans forward and does not look up.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Deliberate effort to keep attention on the breath against the pull of habit.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A demanding stretch in which something must be held against resistance. The card advises persistence in a plain, countable task, and it accepts that some force is needed. Progress shows in the number of unbroken counts, which at first is small.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Forcing the breath. Controlled breathing, strained and shallow, produces tension in the chest and shoulders. Hakuin described the Zen sickness (zenbyō) that follows forced concentration, and in Yasen kanna he prescribed settling the breath in the lower abdomen.

section.label: Links
section.p: IV — Catching the Ox: the same struggle, in the plainest material. V — Herding the Ox: the effort softens into routine.

description.p: Regular, unremarkable practice that holds a day together.

section.label: Stage
section.p: Herding the Ox, in the breath and in movement. Counting gives way to following the breath from start to finish. In kinhin, the short walk between periods of sitting, the sitter learns to take each step with an exhalation and to keep the attention in the soles of the feet.

section.label: Image
section.p: A line of monks in a long corridor, hands folded at the chest, each a half-step behind the last. Light falls through slatted windows onto the floorboards. A single sandal has been left at the end of the corridor.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Steady practice carried from sitting into walking, and from walking into the rest of the day.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Regular, unremarkable practice that holds a day together. The card commends repetition, a fixed pace and the keeping of an agreed form. It names the slow part of the work, when little seems to happen.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Rigid posture and performed seriousness, which turn the form into a display. Walking meditation done for an audience, with a solemn face, has stopped being walking.

section.label: Links
section.p: V — Herding the Ox: the tether is the pace of the step. XV — Ordinary Mind: the later form of discipline that no longer looks like one.

description.p: Effort has settled into fluency.

section.label: Stage
section.p: Riding the Ox Home, in breath and speech. Breath and step agree. Talk comes easily and without self-watching, and the sitter walks home in the evening with no thought about the walk.

section.label: Image
section.p: A traveller on a country road at evening, a flute held loosely in one hand and a breeze lifting the sleeves. Reeds along the verge bend in the same direction as the walker. The road is straight and empty.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Ease between practice and life, with the breath no longer a task.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Effort has settled into fluency. The card suggests that speech, movement and work now agree with each other and that the arrangement can be enjoyed. It recommends not examining the ease too closely.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Taking pleasure in the good state of the breath as an end in itself. The music of the flute becomes the thing to be kept, and the walker begins to guard a mood.

section.label: Links
section.p: VI — Riding the Ox Home: the same ease, in air and gait. VII — The Ox Forgotten: the method is the next thing to be dropped.

description.p: A method has become unnecessary.

section.label: Stage
section.p: The Ox Forgotten, Leaving the Man Alone, in breath. The sitter no longer counts or follows and finds that the breath continues without supervision. The method has done its work and lies unused, like a fishing basket on the bank. One person remains who is sitting, aware of having stopped.

section.label: Image
section.p: A cushion on a wooden veranda with a rosary or counting beads set aside on the floor. A gentle wind moves the paper screens. The seated figure has eyes half-open and faces the garden.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The aid that is no longer needed and can be set down.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A method has become unnecessary. The card suggests putting down a routine, a script or a technique that has served its purpose, and asking what remains afterwards. A sense of quiet satisfaction goes with it.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Pride in having let go of the method, and a refusal to go further. The sitter who has dropped counting can come to think of himself as one who needs no counting.

section.label: Links
section.p: VII — The Ox Forgotten: the device is left behind while the person stays. VIII — The Ox and the Man Both Gone Out of Sight: the one who dropped it is the next to go.

description.p: A clearing in which the usual voice of the self has gone quiet.

section.label: Stage
section.p: The Ox and the Man Both Gone Out of Sight, in breath and speech. There is no one breathing and nothing breathed. The pause between the exhalation and the next inhalation, which the sitter once noticed, is no longer seen as a pause. Talk, if it comes, comes without a speaker.

section.label: Image
section.p: A wide empty sky above a pale horizon. A single bird-shaped gap in a layer of wash, or no bird at all. A faint ring of brush, drawn in one movement, at the centre of the paper.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The cessation of the distinction between breather and breath.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A clearing in which the usual voice of the self has gone quiet. The card names silence that is neither an effort nor a mood, and a pause before any new shape appears. It may be a relief, or it may be an emptiness without content.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Settling into the stillness. Hakuin warned against the cave of the black mountain, where the sitter rests in a silence that changes nothing in daily life.

section.label: Links
section.p: VIII — The Ox and the Man Both Gone Out of Sight: subject and object fall away together. 0 — Mu: the blank that began the sequence.

description.p: A situation is plain and nothing needs to be added to it.

section.label: Stage
section.p: Returning to the Source, in the sounds of the world. Wind in pines is heard as wind in pines. A cough in the hall is a cough, a bell is a bell, and each is complete without a listener adding to it. Speech also returns, with words taken as sounds before they are meanings.

section.label: Image
section.p: A grove of old pines on a hillside, needles drawn in a few hundred fine strokes, mist threading the lower trunks. A small stone lantern stands at the edge, unlit. No figure appears.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Hearing and breathing as parts of the world and not as operations performed on it.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A situation is plain and nothing needs to be added to it. The card suggests listening before speaking and registering what is said without preparing a reply. It names a return to ordinary perception after a period of confusion.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Withdrawal into the grove. A listener who attends to every sound and says nothing leaves the household to run on without him.

section.label: Links
section.p: IX — Returning to the Source: the world appears again, unadorned. X — Entering the Market with Open Hands: what has been heard now has to be answered.

description.p: A readiness to be useful in conversation, correspondence or a shared task.

section.label: Stage
section.p: Entering the Market with Open Hands, in speech and walking. The practitioner walks into a crowd and talks to whoever is there. The words are ordinary, are spoken for the sake of the listener, and carry no trace of the training behind them. The breath is the same as anyone's.

section.label: Image
section.p: A narrow market street under a stretch of cloth awnings that billow in a gust. A barefoot traveller with a gourd on a staff speaks to a fishmonger, who laughs. Paper lanterns and baskets crowd the edges.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Plain speech and easy movement among other people, with no sign of distinction.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A readiness to be useful in conversation, correspondence or a shared task. The card suggests saying the helpful thing in ordinary words and then walking on. It also closes a cycle, and the next card is the first.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Preaching. A word offered from above, however kind, tells the listener that the speaker has something he lacks.

section.label: Links
section.p: X — Entering the Market with Open Hands: the open hand has a voice. I — Searching for the Ox: the cycle returns, and the next search begins from a different footing.

description.p: A person or phase in which silence is the principal fact.

section.label: Rank
section.p: 正中偏 (shōchūhen), the relative within the absolute. In the element of wind, speech and movement are seen through as emptiness first. The person has understood that breath, words and steps arise and fall without anyone owning them.

section.label: Figure
section.p: A monk stands in a courtyard on a day without a breath of air. Hands are folded in front of the chest, the robe hangs straight and the gravel is unmarked. Smoke from an incense stick rises in a column. The face is calm and turned slightly away.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The stillness that follows the first clear seeing of emptiness, and the wind that has dropped.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A person or phase in which silence is the principal fact. The card describes a refusal to speak or to move that has the dignity of insight and some of the quality of retreat. It asks what the stillness is for.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Resting in the calm. Hakuin named this the trap of the first rank, the quiet that is taken for the end of the way, and he ranked it with the dead sitting of the black mountain cave.

section.label: Links
section.p: VIII — The Ox and the Man Both Gone Out of Sight: the emptiness in which the person lingers. IX — Returning to the Source: the wind that has to rise again.

description.p: The significance of a small thing is clear.

section.label: Rank
section.p: 偏中正 (henchūshō), the absolute within the relative. In wind, the plain particulars of weather, sound and walking are met as the whole. A leaf turning over counts as the teaching.

section.label: Figure
section.p: A woman sweeps fallen leaves from a temple path in a light breeze. Some leaves lift as she sweeps and settle again behind the broom. She looks at the ground a few steps ahead and nowhere else.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The recognition of the unconditioned in an ordinary event of air and motion.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: The significance of a small thing is clear. The card describes a person who attends to ordinary detail so closely that it becomes illuminating, and a situation in which the particular is enough. It advises attention to the task nearest at hand.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Cherishing the particular for its beauty and making a devotion of it. Sweeping becomes a ritual of significance and not a way of clearing a path.

section.label: Links
section.p: IX — Returning to the Source: the world seen as it is. XV — Ordinary Mind: the plain thing at hand is the way.

description.p: A response arrives without deliberation and proves to be the right one.

section.label: Rank
section.p: 正中來 (shōchūrai), coming from within the absolute. In wind, speech and action arise out of emptiness without a prior plan, in the way a gust arises from a clear sky.

section.label: Figure
section.p: A wandering monk stops at a ford and calls across the water to a ferryman, one arm raised and the sleeve full of wind. The words are unprepared and the ferryman has turned to listen. The far bank is a pale outline.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: A spontaneous word or movement that answers what the occasion requires.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A response arrives without deliberation and proves to be the right one. The card describes a person who acts from clarity, and a period in which compassion shows itself in a timely remark or a quick step. It advises trusting the response while the occasion is still present.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Mistaking impulse for spontaneity. A person who says whatever comes may do harm and call it freedom from conditioning.

section.label: Links
section.p: XVII — The Shout: speech that cuts through the listener's thinking. XVI — The Wild Fox: spontaneity that ignores cause and effect.

description.p: A conversation or negotiation that goes well because both parties are fully present.

section.label: Rank
section.p: 兼中至 (kenchūshi), arriving at mutual integration. In wind, emptiness and form meet in conversation, in which speaker and listener exchange breath and neither dominates.

section.label: Figure
section.p: Two people stand talking at a crossroads where several roads meet. Their sleeves blow toward each other and a child runs between them with a kite. The conversation has the loose attention of people who are also watching the street.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Full engagement with others, with the two sides of the Rank working together.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A conversation or negotiation that goes well because both parties are fully present. The card describes the ability to listen and to speak in turn, and to adjust without losing a sense of one's own position. It suggests that the exchange itself is the work.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Fluency that turns into skill at managing others. The person who reads every room well can begin to steer it.

section.label: Links
section.p: X — Entering the Market with Open Hands: engaged without separation. XIII — Pacifying the Mind: the mind that no longer needs to be quieted before it can meet another.

description.p: Ordinary competence with nothing left over.

section.label: Rank
section.p: 兼中到 (kenchūtō), unity attained. In wind, breath, step and word are one and leave no mark. The person is in the air as air is in the room.

section.label: Figure
section.p: An old man hangs washing on a line in a steady wind. The sheets fill and snap, and he reaches for the next peg without looking up. A hand fan of the kind used in summer sits in a basket at his feet.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Mature wholeness, with no trace of attainment. Dōgen closes the Genjōkōan with a fan: a monk asks Baoche of Mount Mayu why he fans himself when the nature of wind is constant and reaches everywhere, and Baoche, saying the monk knows only that the wind is constant, goes on fanning.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Ordinary competence with nothing left over. The card describes a person who is not noticed for what he has achieved and who does the day's work without remark. It advises doing what is in front of one.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Being made into an example. Others may treat such a person as a model, and the person may begin to play the part.

section.label: Links
section.p: XV — Ordinary Mind: the way is the daily way. X — Entering the Market with Open Hands: the same figure, with the gourd put down.

description.p: A search is under way for something that is already doing the searching.

section.label: Stage
section.p: Searching for the Ox, in the domain of awareness. A person sits down to find out what is aware and goes looking for it among thoughts, sensations and sounds. Each item found is something that was noticed, so none of them is the noticing.

section.label: Image
section.p: A figure sits in a bare room with a lamp held at arm's length, shining it into the corners. The lamp throws its light across the floor and walls, and the figure's own shadow falls behind. No text.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The first attempt to look for the one who looks. The card names the sense that something is missing and that attention is the place to find it.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A search is under way for something that is already doing the searching. The card marks the start of inquiry and suggests that the questions asked of experience are being asked from within it. Frustration at this point is ordinary.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Making the search a technique and measuring each sitting by whether awareness was located. Equally, concluding from the paradox that inquiry is pointless.

section.label: Links
section.p: I — Searching for the Ox: the same restlessness, here turned inward on the seeker. 0 — Mu: a question that cannot be answered in the terms in which it is asked.

description.p: Early signs that the question has an answer, found in a remark, a pause or an unexpected stillness.

section.label: Stage
section.p: Seeing the Traces, in the domain of awareness. Descriptions of awareness begin to match something in experience. A thought is noticed as it arises, and a gap appears after it before the next one comes.

section.label: Image
section.p: Fresh footprints cross an expanse of smooth sand and stop at the edge of a still pool. The sky is reflected in the pool, and no one stands nearby. No text.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Evidence that awareness is present: the noticing of thoughts, the brief spaces between them, a sentence in a book that describes what happens during sitting.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Early signs that the question has an answer, found in a remark, a pause or an unexpected stillness. The card suggests following the sign and keeping in mind that a description of awareness is a set of marks left behind it.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Mistaking the vocabulary for the experience: learning terms such as witness, ground and presence, and speaking fluently of what has not been seen.

section.label: Links
section.p: II — Seeing the Traces: texts and teachers pointing at what they are not. XI — The Flower and the Smile: recognition that passes without a description.

description.p: A moment of clarity that arrives without effort and cannot be repeated on demand.

section.label: Stage
section.p: Seeing the Ox, in the domain of awareness. A sound is heard, and for a moment there is hearing with no one added to it. The usual commentary falls silent, and awareness is evident as the plain fact of the room.

section.label: Image
section.p: A temple bell has just been struck. Its ring is drawn as a set of widening circles over a quiet courtyard, and a monk on the veranda has turned his head. His face is calm and unreadable. No text.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: A first direct sight of awareness. It shows itself as the condition of everything noticed and not as a further thing to notice.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A moment of clarity that arrives without effort and cannot be repeated on demand. The card advises letting the experience be what it was and refraining from labelling it at once.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Stepping back to watch oneself having the experience, which produces an observer standing behind the awareness and a new search for the observer.

section.label: Links
section.p: III — Seeing the Ox: the sight that comes after the traces. XIII — Pacifying the Mind: looking directly and finding nothing to grasp.

description.p: A good experience is being gripped and is going stale as a result.

section.label: Stage
section.p: Catching the Ox, in the domain of awareness. Having glimpsed awareness, the sitter tries to hold it. Attention narrows, the jaw tightens, and the openness that was seen contracts into a fixed gaze.

section.label: Image
section.p: A hand closes around a shaft of light coming through a window. The light spills through the fingers, and the knuckles are white. The dust in the beam moves unevenly. No text.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The effort to keep an open state in place. Awareness resists being kept, and the attempt produces tension where there had been spaciousness.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A good experience is being gripped and is going stale as a result. The card suggests relaxing the hand and recognising that the openness did not depend on the grip. Some struggle at this stage is expected.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Concluding that the original experience was an illusion because holding it failed, or doubling the effort and sitting with ever greater rigidity.

section.label: Links
section.p: IV — Catching the Ox: the wild mind that resists the rope. XVI — The Wild Fox: the cost of treating insight as something to be possessed.

description.p: Steady practice, or a commitment that needs only to be kept.

section.label: Stage
section.p: Herding the Ox, in the domain of awareness. Sitting becomes a repeated cycle of wandering off, noticing and coming back. Open awareness is practised with less force, and the noticing itself grows quicker and gentler.

section.label: Image
section.p: A herdsman walks a path through tall grass with a loose cord trailing from his hand. The ox, drawn in a few strokes, wanders a little way off and returns without being pulled. The sky above them is left empty. No text.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The long, ordinary work of returning. The card names the sitting that is done day after day with little to show for it, and the gradual softening of the effort.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Steady practice, or a commitment that needs only to be kept. The card suggests that progress here is not visible from one day to the next and that attention is being trained by the returning itself.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Vigilance that turns into policing, in which every lapse is an offence and the sitter becomes the warden of his own mind.

section.label: Links
section.p: V — Herding the Ox: the rope and whip that are held more lightly as the work continues. XV — Ordinary Mind: trying to direct oneself toward the Way turns away from it.

description.p: A phase of calm and competence, in which things that once took labour now go of themselves.

section.label: Stage
section.p: Riding the Ox Home, in the domain of awareness. Open awareness holds without effort, and the sitter rests in it. Thoughts pass through like weather, and the struggle of the earlier stages has lapsed.

section.label: Image
section.p: A boy rides sideways on the back of an ox along a river at dusk, playing a flute. The ox walks on without guidance. Behind them the far bank is a pale line, with no mountains drawn. No text.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Ease in awareness, with the sense of having arrived. The card names the pleasure of sitting that no longer needs defending.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A phase of calm and competence, in which things that once took labour now go of themselves. The card suggests enjoying it and noticing that the ease is still being treated as a possession.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Savouring the peace and sitting in order to return to it, so that a pleasant state replaces the earlier object of the search.

section.label: Links
section.p: VI — Riding the Ox Home: the tune played on the way, in no hurry to arrive. IX — Returning to the Source: the ease of this card, when it no longer depends on a state.

description.p: A technique or a project has done its work and can be set down.

section.label: Stage
section.p: The Ox Forgotten, Leaving the Man Alone, in the domain of awareness. Awareness is no longer an object that is kept or lost. Sitting continues with no one checking whether it is going well, and the sitter is left as the last item of the practice.

section.label: Image
section.p: A man sits on the veranda of a thatched hut in the afternoon, with an empty stall behind him and a rope coiled in the dust. The sky is wide and plain. His eyes are closed, and one hand rests on his knee. No text.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The disappearance of awareness as something to be managed. What remains is a person who is sitting, with a faint sense of himself as the one who has let go.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A technique or a project has done its work and can be set down. The card suggests asking what stays when the method goes, and who is left to ask it.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Pride in effortlessness. The sitter may take rest in his own non-striving for the goal and decline the last step.

section.label: Links
section.p: VII — The Ox Forgotten, Leaving the Man Alone: the tool dropped and the user still present. VIII — The Ox and the Man Both Gone Out of Sight: the person who drops in turn.

description.p: A clearing in which roles and goals have lost their hold.

section.label: Stage
section.p: The Ox and the Man Both Gone Out of Sight, in the domain of awareness. Shikantaza, just sitting, in which Dōgen's instruction is to sit with no aim of becoming a buddha. There is neither a sitter nor something that is aware of sitting, and the stage cannot be reported while it occurs.

section.label: Image
section.p: A single large circle in one brushstroke on pale paper, open at the lower edge where the brush left the surface. Inside it is empty paper, and outside it is empty paper too. No text.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The point at which awareness, its object and its owner all drop away together. The card names the suit's centre and, in this suit, the stage that is closest to the element itself.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A clearing in which roles and goals have lost their hold. The card can mean relief, a pause before a new form, or a blankness that is not yet understanding.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Settling into the blank. Hakuin called this quiet the cave of the black mountain, in which a person sits as if awakened and does not change.

section.label: Links
section.p: VIII — The Ox and the Man Both Gone Out of Sight: the circle itself. 0 — Mu: the same blank, met at the start of the sequence.

description.p: Clear perception after confusion, in which a situation is seen as it is.

section.label: Stage
section.p: Returning to the Source, in the domain of awareness. The sounds and sights of the room are back, and they arise inside an awareness that has nothing added to it. Rain on the roof is heard as rain on the roof.

section.label: Image
section.p: An open window in an empty room looks out on a wet garden. A bowl of water on the sill holds the grey sky, and a maple leaf drifts across the garden. No one is drawn. No text.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Awareness as the field in which things appear, with nothing to separate the field from its contents. The paradox of finding awareness has dissolved without being solved.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Clear perception after confusion, in which a situation is seen as it is. The card suggests that nothing needs adding to what is present, and that the view comes without a method.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Quietism: staying at the window and watching the garden. The verse of the ninth picture also warns that returning to the source is already a step too many.

section.label: Links
section.p: IX — Returning to the Source: streams flowing and flowers red, for no one in particular. XV — Ordinary Mind: the plain world recovered in a master's words.

description.p: Being useful in ordinary company with whatever has been learned, and without comment.

section.label: Stage
section.p: Entering the Market with Open Hands, in the domain of awareness. Awareness goes out into conversation, errands and other people's trouble. It does not call itself awareness, and the person who carries it is hard to tell from anyone else in the queue.

section.label: Image
section.p: A barefoot man in a crowded street stops to hold a door for a woman with a heavy basket. A child looks up at him. Around them the market stalls are drawn in dense detail, and the man alone is painted with few lines. No text.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Awareness used for others and shown only in conduct. The card names attention that is available to whoever happens to be present.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Being useful in ordinary company with whatever has been learned, and without comment. The card marks the end of a cycle, and the next card is the first.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Displaying presence: speaking slowly, gazing meaningfully, offering the calm as a performance. Awareness that announces itself has become an object again.

section.label: Links
section.p: X — Entering the Market with Open Hands: the closing gesture of the whole path. I — Searching for the Ox: the cycle begins again, with the seeker now able to search without distress.

description.p: A phase of detachment that feels like wisdom.

section.label: Rank
section.p: 正中偏 (shō chū hen), the relative within the absolute. In this suit emptiness comes first: awareness is seen to be without content or owner, and the particulars of life appear as thin and passing.

section.label: Figure
section.p: A sitter in a bare room before a blank wall, hands in the cosmic mudra, with the window shuttered. The room is tidy and unlived in. Dust gathers on a closed letter on the floor beside him.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: The clarity of someone who has seen through things. The world is emptied of weight, and nothing in it needs a response.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A phase of detachment that feels like wisdom. The card suggests it is real insight, and that insight of this kind is not yet the whole of the matter.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Resting here. Hakuin warned against the first rank as a trap, a quiet in which realisation is mistaken for withdrawal from the world, and Void is the suit where that trap is the most comfortable.

section.label: Links
section.p: VIII — The Ox and the Man Both Gone Out of Sight: the emptiness that the figure has met. 0 — Mu: the unanswerable question, which this person has stopped hearing as a question.

description.p: Noticing that what was sought elsewhere was present in a routine object or hour.

section.label: Rank
section.p: 偏中正 (hen chū shō), the absolute within the relative. Awareness is recognised in ordinary particulars: a sound, a cup, the grain of a table. The emptiness found earlier is met again in what is in front of the eyes.

section.label: Figure
section.p: A woman at a kitchen table has stopped in the middle of peeling an orange. Light from the window falls on the peel in a long spiral, and she is looking at it with an expression of mild surprise.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Recognition of the open ground in a small thing. The world is back in view, and each part of it shows what the first rank had set aside.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Noticing that what was sought elsewhere was present in a routine object or hour. The card suggests keeping attention on the particular and not hurrying to name what it shows.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Treating the ordinary object as a sign of something more, so that the orange becomes a symbol and the attention moves past it.

section.label: Links
section.p: IX — Returning to the Source: the world seen with nothing added. III — Seeing the Ox: a sight that is quiet and complete.

description.p: An opportunity to act, speak or stay silent from a clear place.

section.label: Rank
section.p: 正中來 (shō chū rai), coming from within the absolute. Action arises out of emptiness. In this suit it is the person who listens with open attention and responds to what is said, with no script prepared.

section.label: Figure
section.p: A nurse sits beside a bed at night with a shaded lamp, one hand lightly on the patient's wrist. Her gaze is on the patient's face, and the window behind her is a dark rectangle.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Compassion that comes from an open mind. The card names attention that has no agenda of its own and is therefore available to what is in front of it.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: An opportunity to act, speak or stay silent from a clear place. The card suggests that the right response is likely to be seen once the self-regarding ones are set aside.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Posing as empty while acting from habit, and calling a reflex spontaneity. The person may also leave their own needs unattended and call it selflessness.

section.label: Links
section.p: X — Entering the Market with Open Hands: help that carries no mark of the helper. XVII — The Shout: a response that comes out before a reply is composed.

description.p: A period in which responsibility and clarity coexist.

section.label: Rank
section.p: 兼中至 (ken chū shi), arriving at mutual integration. Emptiness and form work as two sides of one activity. In this suit the person is fully engaged in affairs and fully open at the same time, and neither side is given up for the other.

section.label: Figure
section.p: A ferryman poles a crowded boat across a river in morning mist. His passengers talk, argue and doze, and he answers each one while he keeps the boat on its line. The far shore is not yet visible.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Competent, wholehearted engagement that rests on open awareness. The work is done well, and the worker is not caught in it.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: A period in which responsibility and clarity coexist. The card suggests that the two need no longer be traded against each other, and that the demands of the present are best met from where one already stands.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Becoming a model of balance, so that the integration is carried as a reputation. The person who has to look integrated has lost the thing.

section.label: Links
section.p: XV — Ordinary Mind: the Way in daily affairs, with no special state. IX — Returning to the Source: the world and the open ground seen as one.

description.p: Quiet completion.

section.label: Rank
section.p: 兼中到 (ken chū tō), unity attained. Wholeness with no trace of attainment. In this suit the paradox of finding awareness has gone, and the person has no view about it and nothing left to say.

section.label: Figure
section.p: An old man sweeps the steps of a small shrine at dawn, in a plain robe. A few leaves lie on the stone. Nothing about him draws the eye, and a visitor passing through the gate would not look at him twice.

section.label: Meaning
section.p: Maturity without display. The practice is not separate from life, and no one, including the person himself, can point to where it is.

section.label: In a reading
section.p: Quiet completion. The card suggests that the matter at hand is done, or nearly so, and that no announcement is needed.

section.label: Pitfall
section.p: Turning the absence of a trace into a style, a studied ordinariness that is another kind of showing. The card can also be misread as the end of the way, when it is the point at which the way is walked without notice.

section.label: Links
section.p: 0 — Mu: the beginning and end of the sequence, here seen as one. XV — Ordinary Mind: the Way that is nothing special.
